In support of his contention the writ petitioner annexed a copy of the representation allegedly made by Afaq Ahmed Khan on 27-7-73 to the then Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar (South) Dhaka (Annexure C) and the copy of the representation dated 2-9-75 allegedly made to the then Minister-in-charge of the Ministry of Public Works for releasing the property from the list of abandoned property (Annexure D), the rent receipt (Annexure B) showing realisation of rent by Afaq Ahmed Khan up to January 1973 from one Mr. Sarowarul Huq, a copy of the application addressed to the Inspector General of Police by Afaq Ahmed Khan for his security and safety of life (Annexure E), a copy of a letter dated 8-9-80 addressed to the writ petitioner from the Public Works and Town Improvement Ministry, Section X for production of the title deed in respect of his claim of title to the disputed property (Annexure F) and the list of the papers submitted to the said Ministry Annexure F1.

6. The learned Judges of the High Court Division by the impluged judgment and order held:

(i) In view of the decree obtained by the writ petitioner on 30-4-86 in Title Suit No. 203 of 1983, the respondent-Government wrongly enlisted the disputed property on 23-9-86 namely, plot No. 16/1, Road-6, Dhanmondi R/A, in violation of the proviso (a) to section 5 of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985;

(ii) Mr. Afaq Ahmed Khan being the owner of both the properties described in Plot Nos.16 and 16/1, Road 6, Dhanmondi RA there is no logic to consider the property of plot No.16 only as an abandoned property.

(iii) Four years having already elapsed since the issuance of Rule Nisi on 22-2-89 in the interest of justice the writ petition cannot be rejected only because of institution of cases in the Court of Settlement in respect of the disputed property, where applications have already been filed by the writ petitioner for withdrawal of those cases.

(iv)In the facts and circumstances of the instant case, rejection of the writ petition on the ground of not availing of an alternative remedy would cause serious prejudice to the writ petitioner.

7. Leave was granted to consider the following submissions:

First, the identity of the writ petitioner and the genuineness of the annexures upon which the writ petitioner claims title to the disputed buildings having been seriously challenged by appellant, whether the High Court Division erred in law in disposing of the writ petition on merit without determining basically those contentious issues including the locus standi of the writ petitioner.

Secondly, the High Court Division, having itself come to the conclusion that the determination of the genuineness of those annexures are not permissible in a writ petition erred in law in not holding that the writ petition was not maintainable;

Thirdly, the writ petitioner having availed of the specific remedy provided in the Special Law i.e. Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 by filing cases in the court of settlement, whether the High Court Division was justified in holding that in the facts and circumstances of the case mere pendency of the cases in the court of settlement does not make the writ petition non-maintainable.

Fourthly, the High Court Division erred in not considering that the writ petitioner did not withdraw the cases from the court of settlement before filing the writ petition.

Fifthly, proviso (a) to section 5 of Ordinance LIV of 1985 cannot mean a decree simpliciter that the building in question is not an abandoned property when the plaintiff admittedly was not in possession thereof at the time of filing of the suit and that the proviso speaks of an executable and/or effective decree and not a decree which is inexecutable;

Sixthly, the declaration of the High Court Division in respect of the building of plot No.16 was uncalled for.

8. As regards the identity of the writ petitioner, Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan the learned Additional Attorney-General, appearing for the appellant-Government, submits that in the cause title of the writ petition Anwar Ahmed son of late Afaq Ahmed Khan has been shown as the petitioner but in the affidavit sworn in support of the writ petition one Md Mosharraf Hosain, son of late Md. Alefresident of No.2, New Bailey Road, PS Ramna, Dhaka has asserted that he himself is the petioner and further the Vokalatnama too has not been executed by Anwar Ahmed Khan, but by Md. Mosharaf Hossain. He therefore submits that the writ petition has been filed in the name of a fictitious person and the same was not at all maintainable. In reply Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for writ petitioner respondent No. 1, submits that no such objection as to the identity of the writ petitioner was raised before the High Court Division and in paragraph 31 of the writ petition, it was asserted that Mr. Mosharaf Hossain is the attorney of the writ petitioner and accordingly he had sworn the affidavit on behalf of the writ petitioner. Mr. Ahmed further submits that the respondents of the writ petition did not also deny in their affidavit-in-opposition the correctness of the assertion made on behalf of the writ-petitioner in the said paragraph 31 of the writ petition.

<u>9. As a matter of long standing practice in the High Court Division, specially in case of writ petition, a person other than the writ petitioner himself has to swear the affidavit in support of the writ petition on behalf of the writ petitioner only with the leave of the Court, provided he can satisfy the Court by producing either the letter of authority or any power of attorney supporting his authority to swear the affidavit. Rule 1 Order 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, referred to by Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, provides that any application or act in or to any court required or authorized by law to be made or done by a party in such court, may, except where otherwise expressly provided by any law for the time being in force, may be made or done by the party in person, or by his recognised agent, or by a pleader appearing, applying or acting, as the case may be, on his behalf.</u>

10. Although certain irregularities are apparent on the face of the writ petition but no objection as to the identity of the writ petitioner was specifically raised by the respondents either verbally or through their affidavit-in-opposition before the High Court Division and, as such, this Division is not inclined to deal with the question of identity of the writ petitioner for the first time.

11. As regards the next point Mr. Bhuiyan submits that on behalf of the respondents of the writ petition genuineness of different annexures annexed with the writ petition was seriously challenged and the High Court Division having itself arrived at the conclusion that the determination of genuineness of those annexures is not permissible in a writ proceeding erred in not holding that the writ petition was not maintainable, as the writ petitioner had sought for relief on the basis of disputed facts. In reply Mr. Ahmed submits that the learned Judges of the High Court Division having, in fact, decided the question involved in the writ petition as to the legality of enlistment of the disputed property in the "Ka" list on the basis of the undisputed decree passed in Title Suit No.203 of 1984 in violation of proviso (a) to section 5 of Ordinance 54 of 1985 it cannot be said that the writ petition was not maintainable.

12. It is true that the High Court Division has proceeded on the basis of the ex parte decree passed on 30-4-86 in the aforesaid title suit declaring the property of plot No. 16/1 not to be an abandoned property where the present appellant was defendant No. 1. But the fact remains that the said decree has been declared void on 8-7-92 in Title Suit No. 77 of 1992 instituted by added respondent No. 5 in which the writ petitioner as well as the Government were defendants. On the date of disposal of the writ petition those facts of non-existence of the said decree were placed before the High Court Division. It was also placed before the High Court Division by added respondent No. 5 that the writ petitioner filed Title Suit No. 204 of 1983 against the Governments order of treating the property of plot No.l6 as an abandoned property but the same was dismissed for default on 26-6-84. The writ petitioner preferred an appeal in the High Court Division, being First Appeal No. 24 of 1984, which was also dismissed for default on 24-11-91 (page 99 PB). It is, however, stated by respondent No.1 in his concise statement that against the decree obtained by respondent 5 in Title Suit No. 77 of 1992, mentioned earlier, the writ petitioner has preferred an appeal in the High Court Division being First Appeal No. 244 of 1992, which is still pending.

13. It appears that the disputed questions namely, the identity of the writ petitioner as the son of the original lessee Afaz Ahmed Khan, the said lessee had been in Bangladesh when the property was declared abandoned property under PO No. 16 of 1972, he was enrolled as an Advocate of Dhaka District Bar, he died in 1975 in Mitford Hospital, Dhaka leaving behind the petitioner and his other sons and a daughter as the claimants of the disputed property, on 27-3-72 the said Afaq Khan himself claimed release of the abandoned property, he subsequently also made representation to the concerned Ministry, etc, could have been properly and effectively resolved in the aforesaid first appeal which is still pending in respect of the suit property.

14. Mr. Bhuiyan also submits that the writ petitioner having already availed of the statutory remedy under Odinance No. 54 of 1985, which is a special law, by instituting cases on 4-1-87 in the court of settlement which have been registered as Case Nos. 12 and 13 of 1993 and the High Court Division itself having found that those cases are still pending, although it is claimed by the writ petitioner that after filing of the writ petition he filed applications for withdrawal of those cases, the learned Judges of the High Court Division erred-in not discharging the Rule solely on the ground that the same was not entertain able.

15. Mr. Ahmed in reply submits that after filing of the cases by the writ petitioner in the Court of Settlement he waited but the said court did not function for a long time which is evident from the fact that about 6 years were required even to register those cases, filed on 4-1-87, and, as such, for adequate and efficacious relief the writ petitioner had to move the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. Mr. Ahmed then submits that having considered the very special facts of the instant case the learned Judges in the interest of justice rightly entertained the writ petition in question and ultimately granted the appropriate relief to the writ petitioner.

<u>16. Ordinance 54 of 1985 has created a special forum to deal with a property which has been enlisted under section 5 as abandoned property. A special procedure has also been made therein to decide those cases. A legal presumption has also been attached under section 5(2) to the list published under sub-section (1) as a conclusive evidence that the enlisted property is an abandoned property. Of course it is a rebutable presumption. The writ petitioner having already availed of the remedy under a special law the High Court Division was not at all justified in declaring that the disputed properties are not abandoned properties only because the Rule Nisi had been obtained as far back as in 1989. Moreover there was no paper before the High Court Division to show that the cases instituted in the Court of Settlement had already been withdrawn either before the institution of the writ petition or before its disposal.</u>

<u>17. In principle where an alternative statutory remedy is available a writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution shall not be entertained to short- circuit the statutory procedure. But there may be exceptional situations where, in spite of statutory provision of an alternative remedy, the High Court Division may find that the alternative remedy is not equally efficatious. In this connection reference may be made to the case of Dhaka Ware House vs Asst. Collector of Customs, 1991 BLD (AD) 227. In the instant case the learned Judges of the High Court Division appear to have misconstrued and misconceived their jurisdiction under Article 102 in holding that the writ petition is maintainable, where the writ petitioner had already availed of the special remedy provided under section 7 of Ordinance No. LIV of 1985.</u>

<u>18. As regards the next point whether the High Court Division correctly appreciated proviso (a) to section 5 of Ordinance NO. LIV of 1985 regarding enlistment of the disputed property in the "Ka list" on 23-9-86 although a decree of the Civil Court was passed on 30-4-86 declaring the property in plot No. 16/1 not to be an abandoned property, it has already been mentioned as to the nature of the decree on the basis of which the High Court Division passed the impugned judgment. The admitted position is that the disputed property was declared as an abandoned property under PO No. 16 of 1972 as far back as in 1972, since when the Government is in possession thereof. Proviso (a) to section 5 contemplates a legally enforceable decree. The ex parte decree obtained by the writ petitioner is a declaratory decree simplicity without any prayer for recovery of possession, when, admittedly, the writ petitioner was not in possession thereof. Such a decree is not within the contemplation of proviso (a) to section 5.</u>

19. In the circumstances we have no hesitation to hold that the learned Judges of the High Court Division patently misconstrued the provision of proviso (a) to section 5 of Ordinance No. LIV of 1985.

20. As regards the last question that the declaration of the High Court Division in respect of the building in plot No.16 was uncalled for, it has already been noticed that the writ petitioner failed to establish that the same was not an abandoned property in Title Suit No. 204 of 1983 which was dismissed on 26-6-84 and the appeal, being First Appeal No. 24 of 1984, was also dismissed on 24- 11-91. On the face of such decisions of the Civil Courts the learned Judges of the High Court Division were not at all justified in declaring the buildings in plot No. 16 also as not an abandoned property.

For the reasons stated above we find substance in this appeal. Accordingly it is allowed without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division are set aside. Writ Petition No. 204 of 1989 is dismissed.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for leave to Appeal No.803 of 1994
lawyer:
Abdul Baset Mujumder, Advocate, instructed by Abul Quasem, Advocate-on-Record ---- For the Petitioners. 
Not represented ---- Respondent.
parties:
AKM Jamaluddin & others ----- Petitioners
vs. 
Mantu Lal Majumder ----- Respondent
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 11-8-94 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.117 of 1993.)
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal J : The plaintiff-petitioners obtained an ex parte decree against the defendant- respondent against which the respondent filed Miscellaneous Case No. 11 of 1992 under Order IX rule 13 CPC which was allowed by the Senior Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong by judgment and order dated 29-10-92 on the ground that although the respondent could not prove that he was ill on the date of hearing and that he merely filed a medical certificate without examining the doctor who issued the certificate, yet his conduct all throughout was diligent and therefore on payment of Taka 1,000.00 to the plaintiff-petitioners within 15 days the suit may be restored to its file.

2. On the plaintiff-petitioner' revision, Civil Revision No.117 of 1993, a Division Bench of the High Court Division found that the procedure adopted by the trial Court will encourage the filing of spurious medical certificates. The doctor who granted the certificate or a witness who knows the doctor's signature should be examined. As such the trial Court's judgment was set aside and the case was sent back on remand to give an opportunity to the defendant-respondent to prove his illness.

3. The plaintiff-petitioners now seek leave to appeal from the aforesaid judgment and order of the High Court Division dated 11-8-94.

4. Mr. A Baset Majumder, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioners, submits that the ex parte decree having been passed after long 7 years from the date of filing of the suit on the failure of the defendant to appear on the date fixed for hearing the application filed under Order IX rule 13 CPC was itself a motivated one and both the Courts having found that the defendant-respondent failed to prove his illness the order of remand is in the nature of giving a premium to the defendant for his laches.

<u>5. As the suit has been restored on payment of compensatory cost to the plaintiff-petitioners we do not think that it is a fit case for interference.</u>

The petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
KS Nabi, Barrister-at-Law with Md Abul Quashem, Md Zakir Hossain, Advocates------For the Petitioner. 
KS Zaman Advocate------For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Abdur Razzaque Mollah  ------ Appellant 
Vs.
Md. Qayum Mollah & others  ------ Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
NK Chakravartty J: This Rule at the instance of defendant-appellant-petitioner was issued calling upon the opposites to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree so far it relates to remand of the case for fresh trial passed in Title Appeal No. 168 of 1996 dated 28th June, 1998 and the decree signed on 2nd July, 1998 by the learned Additional District Judge, Bagerhat reversing and setting aside the judgment and decree dated 18th July, 1996 and decree signed on 23rd July, 1996 passed by the Subordinate Judge, First Court, Bagerhat in Title Suit No. 52 of 1993 should not be set aside, etc.

2. The short facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of this Rule, is that the defendant-appellant-petitioner namely, Mr Abdur Razzaque Mollah is an inhabitant of Bagerhat District and by profession a Barrister-at-Law practicing in London since long. The plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 namely, Md Qayum Mollah is a resident of Bagerhat district and by profession a Contractor. They have previous acquaintance with each other. It is not disputed that the subject matter of the suit is a land as well as the building on it and Mr Abdur Razzaque Mollah is the real owner Mr Abdur Razzaque Mollah desired to construct a dwelling house for his own living at Bagerhat and as he had earlier acquaintance with contractor Md Qayum Mollah; he sought his assistance and that the contractor also agreed to it. Mr Abdur Razzaque Mollah thereafter took loan of Taka 2,00,000 from the defendant No. 3 (opposite party No.2) namely, House Building Finance Corporation, Khulna by mortgaging the said disputed suit land handed over the loan money to the Contractor for the construction of his aforesaid dwelling house at Bagerhat. Later on a dwelling house was constructed but the loan money was not refunded within the stipulated date to the House Building Finance Corporation and as a result of which House Building Finance Corporation instituted a money suit bearing No. 5 of 1991 against Mr A Razzaque and which suit was subsequently decreed ex parte and the House Building Finance Corporation thereafter instituted Money Execution Case bearing No.3 of 1994 for the realisation of loan money from the petitioner Mr Abdur Razzaque Mollah. But in the meantime due to long absence of the Barrister Mr Abdur Razzaque Mollah, plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 managed to create some forged papers alleged to have been executed by Mr Abdur Razzaque Mollah (petitioner) claiming the disputed land and building to have been sold by Mr Abdur Razzaque Mollah to the contractor by way of a deed of agreement for sale i.e. "Bainapatra' and with the ulterior motive the contractor subsequently instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 52 of 1993 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Bagerhat for a decree of Specific Performance of Contract.

3. The short facts of the said case is that, while the defendant No. 1 was owning and possessing the said suit property he proposed to sell the same to the plaintiff who agreed to purchase the suit property at a consideration of Taka 1.10,000 and accordingly, he paid Taka 70,000 to the defendant No.1 on 7-6-1986 and next Taka 25,000 on 9-1-1989 through a cheque and later on 25-1-1989 the balance consideration of Taka 15,000 and that the defendant No. 1 received the entire consideration money. The plaintiff thereafter requested the defendant No. 1 to execute and register the deed of sale but the defendant No.1 did not pay any heed to it. And hence the above noted suit for Specific Performance of Contract. It is the specific case of the plaintiff that he took possession of the suit property from the defendant No.1 as a part performance of the contract.

4. in that suit the defendant No. 3 the House Building Finance Corporation contested by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit property has been under the legal mortgage of the defendant No.3.

5. On the contrary, the defendant No. 1 contested the suit and denied the material allegations of the plaintiff and contended inter alia, that he never executed the bainapatra and the plaintiff by way of fraud and forgery created the same. He has also denied the receipt of the consideration money' of the so-called bainapatra or handed over any possession of the suit property with intent to sell to the plaintiff. The specific case of the defendant No. 1 was that the deed of agreement was forged and manufactured. The plaintiff was a contractor under the defendant No. 1 and he was entrusted to complete the house in question and in the absence of the defendant No.1 the plaintiff got opportunity to enter into the suit building and now he is claiming the property as of his own. The learned Subordinate Judge after trial and hearing the parties decreed the suit in allowing the Specific Performance of Contract.

6. Feeling dissatisfied, the petitioner preferred an appeal before the learned District Judge, Bagerhat and the said appeal was registered as Title appeal No. 168 of 1996. The House Building Finance Corporation also filed another appeal against the said decree bearing No. 183 of 1996. Both the appeals were transferred to the Court of the learned Additional District Judge who heard and disposed of them analogously by a single judgment. The learned Court of appeal below after hearing both the parties set aside the judgment and decree-of the trial Court but remanded back the suit to the trial Court for fresh trial holding that the signatures appearing in the deed of agreement (Exhibit 1) and on other papers such as the signatures upon written statement of the defendant No. 1. deposition sheets etc should be examined through the Handwriting Expert. The learned appellate Court also observed that the trial Court ought not to have based his findings in this inaccurate manner in violation of law when it was the specific case of the defendant No. 1 that the signatures appearing in the bainapatra are forged And, according to the learned appellate Court, the signature of defendant No. 1 and as it appears in bainapatra to have been examined through a hand writing Expert. The learned appellate Court practically reversed the findings of the trial Court.

7. Feeling dissatisfied, defendant No. 1 as petitioner invoked this Court's civil revisional Jurisdiction by laying a petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule with stay.

8. Mr KS Nabi, Barrister-at-Law with Mr MA Kashem, learned Advocates appeared in favour of the defendant-appellant-petitioner and the defendant-opposite party No. 2 is represented by Mr KS Zaman, the learned Advocate and none appeared either to oppose or to support the Rule by the rest of the opposite parties.

<u>9. Mr KS Nabi, the learned Advocate submits that the impugned judgment and decree of remand for fresh trial of the suit by the appellate Court is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice since the appellate Court has by the order acted contrary to law as it can decree the suit under section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure or it can refuse the specific performance as a Court of first instance without relegating the parties in the proceedings again for fresh trial. According to Mr SK Nabi, the appeal is the continuation of the suit it is continued and reheard the fresh trial of fresh hearing de novo is contrary to law and thus the impugned judgment and decree is an error of law in its decision occasioning failure of justice. He has further submitted that the relief of Specific Performance is discretionary of the Court and section 22 of the Specific Relief Act provides clearly that Court is not bound to grant such relief earlier because it is lawful to do so, in remanding back the case the exercise of the discretion by the trial Court is redundant as the appellate Court has already exercised the said discretion and set aside the decree reversing the findings of facts and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is an error in its decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr KS Nabi, the learned Advocate finally, argued that the trend of justice structure and judicial management is to saving the costs of the litigation and to prevent the protracted litigation and, as such, remand order was unjust which is liable to be set aside. In this connection he has referred two rulings reported in 43 DLR (AD) 78 as well as 43 DLR (AD) 125 wherein their learned Lordships held:</u>

<u>"Remand-When revisional Court need not pass order of remand-The revisional application could be disposed of by the High Court Division without sending the case on remand to the trial Court. Both oral and documentary evidence having been available on record there was no necessity for the remand as ordered by the High Court Division. i.e. the principle laid down in a case of remanding the appeal or revision, etc."</u>

10. Mr KZ Zaman, the learned Advocate appeared by executing a fresh power in favour of the opposite party No. 2 (defendant No. 3), House Building Finance Corporation, Khulna and submits that the learned judge of the appellate Court by the elaborate discussion of evidence having found that the judgment and decree of the trial Court were illegal, invalid and he having rightly set aside the judgment and decree appealed against, he should have dismissed the suit on merit and the order of remand for giving chance to the plaintiff for proving his case by producing fresh evidence cannot be sustained in law as because the suit property was already mortgaged to House Building Finance Corporation. That even in the case of genuine agreement for purchase, the plaintiff is not entitled to get specific performance after long 15 years gap at a shockingly low price which being intolerable hardship on the part of the defendant-appellant- petitioner, the plaintiffs suit is liable to be dismissed in which case no benefit will be obtained by sending the case on remand for fresh trial except loss of valuable time and money of the parties. That admittedly the suit properties having been mortgaged to House Building Finance Corporation defendant No.3 against loan of Taka 2,00,000 for construction of residential house in the suit land and the said defendant No.3 having obtained decree for the said amount in Artha Rin Suit No. 5 of 1991 against the defendant No.1, the instant suit for specific performance for the self same properties is not maintainable in law and the learned Additional District Judge of the Appellate Court ought to have dismissed the suit instead of sending the suit on remand for fresh trial.

11. Keeping in view the above argument let me address myself to resolve the controversy whether the petitioner could make out a case for reversal of the findings and decision of the Courts below on the ground that they committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in disbelieving the claim of the defendant-petitioner regarding denial of execution of any agreement whatsoever for the sale of the suit property and receipt of the consideration money, if any, from the plaintiff and thereby adopted two different views in assess merit of the instant case.

12. Let 'me now turn to the facts and circumstances adduced from both the sides. The alleged basic contract on the basis of which the suit was filed is the deed of agreement (Bainapatra), which is marked (Exhibit-l) to prove the case of the plaintiff he has examined 3 witnesses including himself as PW 1, on the contrary, the defendant No. 1 petitioner examined 4 witnesses including himself as DW 1. Both sides filed some documents, which were marked Ext. 1-2(2) and 'Ka-Ga'(l ) in support of their respective cases. On the other hand, Defendant No.3 also examined 2 DWs and filed some documents marked Ext. 'Gha-Gha (18). PW 1 Md Qayum Mollah has said that at the time of execution of the deed of agreement his friend Md Nasir was present. But Md Nasir was not produced for examination as a witness. He has also stated that possession of the suit land was given to him by the defendant No. 1 But there appear no other corroborative witness in support of his contention. PW 2, Sheikh Mukbul Haque, is a deed writer of Bagerhat Sub-Registrar Office and PW 3, Shudangshu Kumar Biswas is an attesting witness of the deed of agreement and the money receipt (Ext 2) They have not stated anything about the possession. According to these PWs, the document was read over to the executant in his presence but in the document Exhibits 1 and 2 there are no such statements in writing that the document was read over. So this Parole Evidence is not admissible in evidence. Considering their entire testimony it appears to us that they are tutored and deposed like a parrot.

13. On the other hand, DW Mr Abdur Razzak Mollah has stated in his deposition that he has not received any money from the plaintiff as advance consideration by executing Exhibits 1 and 2. But he received a loan amount of Taka 25,000 which he paid back in due time to the plaintiff. He has totally denied the execution of the bainapatra (Exhibit-1) and signature appearing in the bainapatra and also in Exhibit-2 is not of his own. According to him, signatures are forged and fabricated because of the fact that he being a barrister full time engaged in his legal profession as of a legal practitioner in England and Wales. Mr KS Nabi, the learned Advocate, under the facts and circumstances, apprised us to the facts that a contractor who was employed to develop the residential building construction of the defendant No. 1 has created documents to grab the suit property by the Court's process. Moreover, the bainapatra has no probative value and, according to him, this bainapatra is hit under section 49 of the Registration Act as void.

14. In the instant revisional application we find that being aggrieved by the decree of suit No. 52 of 1993 defendant No. 1 preferred appeal being Title Appeal No. 168 of 1996 and the defendant No. 3 (opposite party No. 2) the House Building Finance Corporation also preferred an appeal being Title Appeal No. 183 of 1996 before the learned District Judge, Bagerhat and both the appeals were subsequently transferred to the Court of learned Additional District Judge, Bagerhat who heard and disposed of them analogously by one single, judgment. The learned Lower Court of appeal after hearing both the parties set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court but remanded back the suit to the trial Court for fresh trial. It transpires from the findings and decision of the Court of appeal below that in passing of the judgment and order he has observed that the signatures appearing in the deed of agreement and on the other papers, such as on the written statements of the defendant No.1, deposition sheets. etc on the basis of which under section 73 of the Evidence Act the trial Court found the bainapatra as genuine. are forged and not genuine. The trial Court ought not to have based his finding in this inaccurate manner and then the trial Court has violated the law. The signatures are forged according to the Court of appeal below but the learned appellate Court wants to get the signatures examined by handwriting expert, when the lower Court of appeal has reversed the findings and it is a concluded fact which need not be opened again for protracting litigation for time immemorial. And thus ordering to send back the case on remand for fresh trial the lower appellate Court has committed an error of law. When all evidences and materials on record were before the appellate Court; the appellate Court could have decided the case itself without remanding it to fresh trial by the trial Court and we also find support of this view in reported case AIR 1975 All 341. In such similar facts and circumstances of the case we also find support in the case of Ram Chand Appellant vs Ram Swarup Respondent reported in AIR 1952 Allahabad 654 where it is held:

"An appeal is not a distinct proceeding from the suit but a further continuation of the suit started in the Court first instance and when an appeal is filed against a decree passed by the Court of first instance in a suit the suit is removed to the Court of appeal and continued and reheard there."

<u>15. So, there is hardly any scope for fresh trial while the judgment and decree are set aside. This appellate Court thus acted erroneously and the impugned order has occasioned failure of justice. Section 22 of the Specific Relief Act clearly provides that the jurisdiction to decree Specific Performance is discretionary; and the Court is not bound to grant such relief merely because it is lawful to do so. This has also been settled in the case of Jalaluddin Mia vs Md Yousuf reported in 1982 BCR 270. The relief of Specific Performance of Contract is a discretionary one. The Court if it finds that it would be unconscionable to allow it will not allow Specific Performance. So, the appellate Court while allowing to set aside the decree ought not to have relegated the defendant No.1 again for facing fresh trial for sanction.</u>

16. Let me now turn to the 2nd contention advanced on behalf of the defendant No. 3 (opposite party No. 2) by Mr KS Zaman, the learned Advocate. He has pointed out before us the President's Order No. 7 of 1973, The Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation Order, 1973 of Article 21(3) which runs thus:

"No property shall be accepted as security unless it is free from all encumbrances and charges and it shall be one of the terms upon which the loan shall be made that the property and the house in respect of which the loan is made shall not be sold or charged without the prior approval of the Corporation and any sale, transfer made or charge or encumbrance created without the approval of the Corporation, in respect of such property shall be null and void."

17. From the facts and circumstance of the case and the evidence on record it appears that the suit properties had been mortgaged before hand to defendant No.3, the House Building Finance Corporation against loan case No. Bag-8 of 1985 for loan of Taka 1,00,000.00 for constructing house on the suit land within the knowledge of the plaintiff and the Mortgagee having obtained a decree in Artha Rin Adalat Suit No.5 of 1991 in the Court of Sub-Judge cum Artha Rin Adalat, Bagerhat the instant suit for Specific Performance of Contract over the self same properties is not maintainable in law and plaint of this suit liable to be rejected under Order VII rule II. Civil Procedure Code and, as such the order of remand is liable to be set aside and the suit is liable to be dismissed for the ends of justice; for that even in case of genuine agreement for alleged purchase, the plaintiff is not entitled to get decree of Specific Performance after long gap of 15 years within which period the price of the suit properties has gone up several hundred times and specific performance has become intolerable hardship for the defendant-petitioner and the Court is not likely to exercise its discretionary power in passing Decree for Specific Performance and the order of remand is improper and illegal; for that the plaintiff having utterly failed to prove his alleged contract for sale by legal evidences, his suit is liable to be dismissed and the order of remand giving him opportunity to prove his case by fresh evidence cannot be sustained in law. This aspect of the matter escaped the notice of the trial Judge as well as the Courts of appeal below resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

18. On the examination of decision, reason and conclusion reached by the learned Additional District Judge, Bagerhat it can be said that those are tainted with illegality, legal infirmity and fragrant error of facts and law warranting interference by this Court in the exercise of Civil Revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

19. In the result, this Rule arising out of Civil Revision Petition got merit and the same thus, stands absolute. The impugned judgment and decree so far it relates to remand of the case for fresh trial passed in Title Appeal No. 168 of 1996 dated 28th June, 1998 decree signed on 2nd July, 1998 by the learned Additional District Judge, Bagerhat reversing and setting aside the judgment and decree dated 18th July, 1996 decree signed on 23rd July, 1996 passed by the Subordinate Judge, First Court, Bagerhat in Title Suit No. 52 of 1993 are hereby set aside. Consequently, Title Suit No. 51 of 1993 is dismissed.

20. Under the facts and circumstances of the case, we direct the parties to bear their respective costs all through.

Send down the lower Court's Record immediately.

End.

lawyer:
Md Waliur Reza Chowdhury, Advocate------For the Petitioner. 
Md Hannan with Md Mainul Islam and AB Showkat Ali, Advocates------For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Ismail (Md)  ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Motasim Ali Chowdhury  ------ Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
The subject matter of challenge in this Civil Revision petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is an order dated 24-3-1999 recorded by Second Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka in Title Suit No.226 of 1985 allowing an application under Order 26 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The decision proposed to be given in this civil Revision petition does not demand a detailed recounting of facts except that sole opposite party No.1 of this Civil Revision petition as sole plaintiff laid a suit being Title suit No. 326 of 1982 in First Court of Munsif, Dhaka for declaration of title and recovery of Khas possession with respect to property described in schedule to the plaint. The said suit was renumbered as Title Suit No. 226 of 1985 on transfer to the Second Court of Assistant Judge Dhaka.

3. Plaintiff opposite party on 26-5-1985 presented an application for Local Investigation under Order 26 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure by a Survey Knowing Advocate of the court on the following points:

(i) to ascertain the western boundary line of CS Plot No.110 of Mouza Tejkunipara and eastern boundary line of CS Plot No.935 of the same Mouza.

(ii) to show the suit land on the western part of CS Plot No. 110 as shown by letters ABC and don the hand sketch with schedule to the Plaint.

4. Mr Md Abdur Rashid having been appointed Advocate Commissioner held Local investigation as prayed for and submitted his report. The report submitted by learned Advocate Commissioner on the above Local Investigation was rejected on objection.

5. Defendant-petitioner on 15-1-1986 laid an application for Local Investigation under Order 26 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure on three points.

(i) To, relay the plaintiff’s deed to ascertain whether plaintiff is in possession of the area covered by his purchase deed or Much land in his possession.

(ii) to relay whether' defendant is possessing any land in excess of the land purchased by him.

(iii) To note the physical features of the lands and to submit map and field book, etc.

6. The report submitted by the learned Advocate Commissioner on the above subject matters of local investigation was accepted by the court on 8-1-1987. Plaintiff opposite party, thereafter, presented another application for Local investigation under Order 26 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for Local Investigation on two points which was exactly the same subject matter of Local investigation dated 26-5-1985. Investigation was held through a learned Advocate Commissioner and report was submitted by learned Advocate Commissioner.

7. Learned Assistant Judge on 3-6-1989 recorded order that the said report would be considered at the time of disposal of suit and fixed 18-6-1989 for peremptory hearing.

8. Plaintiff opposite party thereafter on 14-3-1999 prayed for Local Investigation under Order 26 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the subject matter of Local Investigation sought by plaintiff in earlier two applications dated 26-5-1985 and 9-4-1987. Language and words of the subject matters of Local Investigation though not exactly in the same language and words couched in earlier two applications for Local Investigation but the substance of subject matters remained the same.

9. Defendant-petitioner resisted the said application on laying a written objection taking the stand that the application for Local Investigation was the repetition of the earlier applications on the same subject matters and the application had been directed only to cause delay of disposal of the suit.

10. Learned Assistant Judge by the order under challenge in the Civil Revision petition allowed the same. In recording that order the learned Assistant Judge only held that to secure ends of justice the prayer was allowed.

11. Feeling dissatisfied the defendant petitioner invoked this court's Civil Revisional Jurisdiction on laying a petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule.

12. Mr Md Aliur Raza Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appeared in support of the civil revision petition. The plaintiff opposite party is represented by Mr Md Hannan along with Mr Md Mainul Islam and Mr AB Showkat Ali, the learned Advocates.

13. Heard the learned Advocate, perused the impugned order and other papers annexed in the Civil Revision petition as well as the supplementary affidavit filed by the defendant petitioner and other papers placed before me.

<u>14. From the materials on record it appears that the application for Local Investigation under Order 26 rule, 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure presented by the plaintiff-opposite party on  9-4-1987 was allowed. A survey trained Advocate was appointed who held Investigation and submitted his report. Learned Assistant Judge instead of recording any order either of acceptance or rejection kept the matter pending for consideration at the time of final hearing. Learned Assistant Judge was required to dispose of the Local Investigation matter whether he would reject the same or accept before posting the suit for peremptory hearing. It appears that learned Assistant Judge shirked his responsibility in not disposing the Local Investigation matter. It has already been stated that the subject matter of Local Investigation in the application dated 9-4-1987 and the application dated 14-3-1999 were exactly same in substance. Since the Local Investigation matter was pending before the court for consideration by it at the time of final hearing of the suit, he was not at all justified in allowing the prayer of Local Investigation dated 14-3-1999. Learned Assistant Judge also in recording the impugned order did not assign any reason whatsoever and allowed the application for Local Investigation simply stating that for ends of justice the prayer stood allowed. The said order cannot be characterised to be a speaking order and it also cannot be said that the learned Judge had applied his judicial mind to resolve the controversy. The approach made by the learned Judge appears to be a very flippant approach and does not appear to be intelligible.</u>

15. Since the Local Investigation matter was very much pending before the court it was required to be disposed of before pre-emptory hearing. It is informed by the learned lawyers of both the sides that in view of special consideration the testimony of defendant No.1 as DW 1 was recorded and the testimony of plaintiff as PW 1 was partly recorded. The suit is of the year 1982. Long 18 years has already elapsed since the commencement of the proceeding. Justice demands that the suit is to be disposed of as expeditiously as possible and a direction is accorded below. I am informed by the learned Advocate from the side of the defendant petitioner that direction was recorded by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.826 of 1989 which was directed against an order allowing amendment of the plaint at the instance of the plaintiff opposite party to dispose of the suit within 3 months from the date of receipt of the record. But that direction recorded by the High Court Division was not complied with. The certified copy of the judgment dated 13th January 1993 recorded by the High Court Division had been placed before me. On Perusal of the judgment I find that the High Court Division directed the trial Court to conclude trial within 3(three) months from the receipt of the order of the court.

16. Learned Assistant Judge is directed to dispose of the report submitted by learned Advocate Commissioner on 16-11-1988 within 1(one) month from the date of receipt of this order. Learned Assistant Judge is also directed to dispose of the suit within two months of the disposal of the Advocate Commissioner's report positively. Learned Assistant Judge is also directed not to grant any adjournment to any of the parties.

17. With recording of the above observation I record a further order which is that Learned Assistant Judge, Dhaka at the relevant time who was the presiding judge is directed to show cause within 1(one) month of the receipt of this order to show cause as to why he shall not face the proceeding for non-compliance of the positive order recorded by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.826 of 1989. The show cause is to be submitted to the Registrar of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, Dhaka within that period.

18. A copy of this judgment be served upon the learned Assistant Judge at the relevant time.

19. A copy of this judgment be transmitted to the learned District Judge Dhaka.

20. On conspectus the Rule is made absolute.

The impugned order dated 24-3-1999 is set aside.

21. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of Rule on 23-5-1999 stands vacated.

Having regard to the fact and circumstances of the case I direct the parties to bear their respective costs.

End.

caseno: Civil Revision No. 2612 of 2001 with Civil Revision No. 2617 of 2001
lawyer:
Garib Newaz, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Nazrul lslam with Md Taj Mohammad, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Parties
parties:
Delwar Hossain Khan ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Alhaj Rustom Ali and others ----- Opposite Prties
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: This order will dispose of both the Rules, which arise out of the following facts and circumstances:

2. On 8-11-1994 opposite party Nos. 1 to 9 in the earlier Rule made an application under Order XXI rules 100 and 101 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka against the petitioner for restoration of possession of 13 decimals of land of plot No. 447 comprising of municipal holding No. 185 West Agargaon. The application was numbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 39 of 1994. Then, on transfer to the Court of Additional Subordinate Judge, Dhaka the case was re-numbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 8 of 1995.

3. Their case, in short, is that in 1926 Moina Prasad Chowdhury being owner in possession in 14.42 acre of land of CS plot Nos. 447, 448 and 495 appertaining to CS khatian Nos. 50, 51, 52, 53 and 54 at present of Mohammadpur transferred, 2.06 acre of land to Abbad Ali alias Abbas Fakir by a registered deed No. 2648. Similarly, Moina Chowdhury exhausted all his interest in said land by transfer of 2.06 acres each to other six persons 2.06 acre of land was recorded in khatian No. 35 in SA record of rights in the name Of Abbas Fakir who then died leaving his heirs and legal representatives. By successive transfer, Golam Rahman and Mohammad Hossain acquired 16½ decimals of land of plot No. 447 by registered deed No. 1721 and 1977 dated 27-7-1977 and 12-7-1977. Then, out of said land, Golam Rahman and Mohammad Hossain transferred 13 decimals of Johura Khatun, mother of said opposite parties by two deeds being No. 18959 and 18960 dated 26-5-1978 Johura Khatun filled the land with earth, erected 6 feet high boundary walls and tin roofed house with pucca lavatory, bathroom, kitchen and four verandas, and let out to tenants. She got her name mutated in the revenue record as well as in the municipality, water and gas connection and possessed on payment of various rates, rents and taxes, and also through tenants. In October, she died leaving said opposite parties as husband, sons and daughters.

4. In Title Execution No. 29 of 1993 by executing a collusive and fraudulent decree, on 5-11-1994 the petitioner evicted opposite parties from said land with the help of the police and goons. Opposite parties were not made parties in the suit or in the execution. The petitioner or his predecessor had never any right, title or possession in said land.

5. Same date, that is 8-11-1994, similarly, opposite party Nos. 1 to 4 in the latter Rule also made similar application under Order XXI rules 100 and 101 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the same executing Court against the petitioner for restoration of possession of 8¼ decimals of land of plot No. 447 comprising of municipal holding No. 158 West Agargaon and 16½ decimals of same plot comprising of municipal holding No. 157 West Agargaon at present holding Nos. 157, 15711 and 157/2. The application was numbered as miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 1994. Then, on transfer to the Court of Additional Subordinate Judge, Dhaka the case was re-numbered as Miscellaneous Case No.9 of 1995.

6. Their case, in short, is that in 1926 Moina Prasad Kairi being owner in possession in 14.42 acre of land of CS plot No. 447, 448 and 495 appertaining to CS khatian Nos. 50, 51, 52, 53 and 54 of present Mohammadpur transferred 2.06 acre of land to Abbas Ali alias Abbas Fakir by a registered deed No. 2648. Similarly, said Moina Prasad exhausted all his interest in said land by transfer of 2.06 acre each to other six persons, 2.06 acre of land was recorded in khatian No. 35 in SA record of rights in the name of Abbas Fakir who then died leaving his heirs and legal representatives. Out of said land, Abdul Kadir and Abdul Rashid by deed Nos. 8886 and 8882 dated 1-6-1966 acquired some land, and then, transferred 8½ ,decimals of land by deed No. 18734 dated 26-5-1978 to Aleya Huda. Abdul Kader by another deed dated 26-5-1978 transferred 16½ decimals of land to Johura Khatun, mother of opposite party Nos. 2 to 4 and delivered possession. Opposite Party No. 1 Aleya Huda and Jahura Khatun by demarcating their respective lands with boundary walls and erecting huts possessed through tenants and on payment of rates, rents and taxes.

7. On 2-8-1989 said Jahura Khatun gifted said 6½ decimals of land to her daughters, opposite party Nos. 2 to 4 and getting possession, opposite party Nos. 2 to 4 got their names mutated in the revenue record and the municipality and possessed through tenants on payment of rents, taxes and rates.

8. On 5-11-1994 the petitioner by executing a collusive and fraudulent compromise decree obtained forceful possession of said land with the help of police and goons, demolishing the structures and boundary walls worth Taka 30,000 and looting goods worth Taka 50,000 from their purchased land.

9. The petitioner opposed both the applications by filing separate but similar written objections. His case, in short, is that the applications are not maintainable. The land of plot Nos. 447 and 448 originally belonged to Krishna Kamini Chowdhurani, who died leaving a son, Sudhanya Roy Chowdhury. Three sons, namely, Sunil, Anil and Makhan, survived Sudhanya, Anil died unmarried and Makhan died at the hands of Pak Army. Their shares devolved upon Sunil, who died leaving two sons, Danu and Manuj. Manuj led no family life. Danu gave a power of attorney to one Shahidullah and said Shahidullah entered with the petitioner into agreement to sell. Then, the petitioner instituted Title Suit No. 59 of 1992 for specific performance of contract and got a sole decree. In execution of the decree in Title Execution No. 29 of 1993, on 5-11-1994 the petitioner got possession of the land through Court. Opposite parties were never in possession of the land nor did they have any title to the land. Opposite parties could not get any relief without partition.

10. The cases were heard separately. Opposite parties examined four witnesses in each of the cases, adduced number of documents, which were marked as exhibits No. 1 to 13 in the earlier case and exhibits No. 1 to 15 in the latter one. But the petitioner did neither examine any witness nor any documents in any of the cases. An Advocate Commissioner was appointed for ascertainment of the dispossessed land.

11. Learned Subordinate Judge disposed of-the cases by one judgment. On consideration of the evidence on record, learned Subordinate Judge held that opposite parties were in possession of the land before they were dispossessed on 5-11-1994 in execution, and that they were not judgment debtors nor did they claim through the judgment debtors. Upon such findings, the executing Court allowed the applications and directed the petitioner to restore possession within thirty days by impugned order.

12. Against the impugned order, the petitioner obtained the above Rules.

<u>13. Mr Garib Newaz, for the petitioner, mainly submits that the application of the claimants are not maintainable and the executing Court erred in law in allowing the same when, the land claimed by the claimants is not covered by the decree. He relied upon the decisions in the cases of Bholanath Bondopadhyaya vs Banarsilal Saraf, AIR 1961 Assam 79 and MP Mishra vs Sangam Lal Agarwal AIR 1975 All 424. He also submits that the learned Advocate Commissioner also could not ascertain the land.</u>

14. Opposing the Rule, an affidavit-in-opposition annexing number of papers was filed on behalf of the opposite parties. Mr Nazrul Islam submits that the petitioner sought execution of a collusive and fraudulent decree in respect of 1.60 acre out of 5.20 acres of land of three plots without any specification, boundary and quantity of land from each of the plots. Advocate Commissioner was appointed mainly to ascertain through local inspection whether there were any dwelling structures on the said land in order to make an application for injunction to restrain the petitioner from making any change in the nature and character of the land fill disposal of the case. On due consideration of the evidence, oral and documentary, as adduced by the claimants and the report of the learned Advocate Commissioner, he further submits, the executing Court correctly found the claimants in possession of the land on their own rights before dispossession by the Court and that the claimants were not judgment debtors and upon such findings, ordered restoration of possession, which does not call for any interference.

15. Only issue before us is, whether the executing Court was wrong in exercise of the discretion under Order XXI rule 101 of the Code in allowing the applications. In order to appreciate the submissions of the learned Advocates, we should first consider the relevant provisions, Order XXI rules 100 and 101 of the Code, which reads:

"100. (1) Where any person other than the judgment-debtor is dispossessed of immovable property by the holder of a decree for the possession of such property or, where such property has been sold in execution of a decree, by the purchaser thereof, he may make an application to the Court complaining of such dispossession.

(2)  The Court shall fix a day for investigating the matter and shall summon the party against whom the application is made to appear and answer the same.

101. Where the Court is satisfied that the applicant was in possession of the property on his own account or an account of some person other than the judgment-debtor, it shall direct that the applicant be put into possession of the property."

16. To conceive the purport of the above provisions in contradistinction from other provisions under Order XXI relating to delivery of possession of immovable property in execution of a decree, few things must be noted first. no execution can proceed against a person who is not a judgment-debtor or who does not claim through any judgment-debtor. Secondly, no execution can validly proceed against any property other than immovable property and not covered by the decree.

<u>17. Rule 100 has given a fight to a person, who is not a judgment-debtor yet is dispossessed of immovable property in execution of a decree to make an application complaining of such dispossession. Here the words immovable property must be discerned as not movable property. Rule 101 requires of an executing Court to investigate in order to be satisfied as to whether the applicant was in possession of the property as complained of and secondly, if such claimant was in possession on his own account or on account of some person who was not the judgment-debtor. When the Court finds the answer in the affirmative, it becomes the duty of the Court to put the claimant back into possession at once. The proceedings under the rules are no doubt summary in nature and the wrong done to a party by the executing Court at the instance of the decree holder without any fault of such party, must be remedied by the executing Court without any further delay.</u>

18. We have gone through all the evidence and the papers relied upon by the parties. It appears that on 23-3-1992 the petitioner instituted Title Suit No. 59 of 1992 against one Dasu Roy Chowdhury represented by one Md Shahidullah Mia for specific performance of an agreement for sale. He made out the case that said Shahidullah as an attorney entered into the agreement with the petitioner for sale of 1.60 acre out of 5.20 acre of land of plot Nos. 447, 448 and 495 appertaining to khatian No. 50 of present mouje Mohammadpur and on receipt of Taka 15,000, executed and registered an agreement. Then, on 14-10-1991 Shahidullah received further Taka 1,00,000. On 29-7-1992 the petitioner and said Shahidullah made a joint application for compromise. On 14-9-1992 the suit was decreed on compromise. On 21-9-1992 the decree was signed. Then, on 6-11-1993 the petitioner levied the decree in Title Execution Case No. 29 of 1993 for possession of 1.60 acre out of 5.20 acre of land of plot Nos. 447, 448 and 495. On 8-3-1994 the petitioner made an application for police help for possession. Then, the executing Court allowed by its order dated 28-5-1994 an amendment by replacing plot No. 484 in place of plot No. 448. Again on 26-10-1994 the petitioner applied for police force. On 3-11-1994 the petitioner applied for direction to the Bailiff to deliver possession by breaking open the doors, if necessary. The same date a writ of delivery of possession was issued to deliver possession by breaking open the doors if so needed. On 5-11-1994 the process server reported that he delivered possession of 1.60 acre out of 5.20 acre of plot Nos. 447, 484 and 495 by removing all movables. On 8-11-1994 the petitioner made an application for dropping the execution proceedings since the effectiveness of the execution was over.

19. In the application for execution, the petitioner applied for possession of 1.60 acre out of 5.20 acre of land of plot Nos. 447, 448 and 495. We could not find any description or identification of said land in the application. The report of the process server also does not show possession of what quantum of land from which plot was delivered. The executing Court however, finds that 1.30 acre of plot Nos. 447 and 30 decimals of plot No.484 were delivered. After two years of commencement of the execution plot No. 484 was substituted in place of plot No. 448 and land of plot No. 495 was already acquired.

<u>20. We further find that the claimants have convincingly proved that they were owners in possession on their own in their land of plot No. 447 by evidence, oral and documentary, and on 5-11-1994 they were dispossessed in execution of the aforesaid decree by the petitioner. They were neither judgment-debtors nor they claimed through the judgment debtor. One of the witnesses is a neighbour and two were tenants, and another was a ward commissioner. The executing Court could not find any reason to disbelieve the witnesses. Besides, on 14-2-1995 the Advocate Commissioner reported that he did not receive any co-operation from the petitioner yet he could identify the land. It may be noted that the commissioner was appointed for local inspection not for local investigation. The application of the petitioner before the executing Court dated 3-11-1994 and the order passed thereupon clearly supports the case of the claimants that they had dwellings on their land possession of which was taken by the petitioner in execution. On the contrary, the petitioner could not adduce an iota of evidence whatsoever. In the circumstances and on the evidence, the executing Court was satisfied that the claimants were in possession of the land on their own and on 5-11-1994 were dispossessed in execution process, and accordingly, it directed for restoration. We could not find any error in the exercise of jurisdiction by the executing Court in allowing the applications made under Order XXI rules 100 and 101 of the Code.</u>

21. The submission of Mr Garib Newaz that the land from which the claimants were dispossessed is not covered by the decree and the applications of the claimants therefore are not maintainable under Order XXI rule 100 of the Code is wholly misconceived. The petitioner obtained a decree for possession of land of plot No. 447 amongst others. He also got possession of land of plot No. 447 in execution of the decree. The petitioner failed to adduce any evidence against the proof of the claimants that they were dispossessed from their land of plot No. 447

<u>22. In Bholanath Bondopadhyaya vs Banarsilal Saraf, AIR 1961 Assam 79, the applicant claimed that in the process of execution the decree holder had got into possession of two strips of his land beyond the decreed land. Facts were though accepted but the application was rejected holding the same was not maintainable. A single bench of Assam High Court held that</u>

<u>"In my opinion the words 'such property' would mean the property covered by the decree and not any other property and in the particular case the petitioner was dispossessed not of property covered by the decree but of some other property which is not covered, in my opinion, by the words 'such property' occurring in the Rule as quoted above. I therefore agree with the learned Subordinate Judge that Order XXI, rule 100, Civil PC has no application to the facts of the case."</u>

<u>23. MP Mishra vs Sangam Lal Agarwal. AIR 1975 All 424, is case of excessive execution. The applicant claimed that in execution of the decree the decree holder had obtained possession not only over a portion of decreed house No. 15-A but also over a portion of house No. 15 of which he was owner in possession. A Division Bench of Allahabad High Court held:</u>

<u>"We are unable to accept the contention of learned Counsel for the appellant that the expression 'decree for possession of such property' refers to a decree for the possession of any immovable property. The language of sub- rule (1) of Rule 100 is clear and a plain reading thereof shows that the expression 'such property' refers to the immovable property from which the person making the application has been dispossessed. That being so, the application filed by the appellant was not maintainable under Order XXI rule 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure."</u>

24. The case before us is not one of excessive execution and, as such, the above cases have no manner of application. When factually it is found that the petitioner took possession of land of the claimants of plot No. 447 in execution of the decree which includes said land through a writ of delivery of possession, we do not need to express our opinion more than what was stated above on the interpretation of the words 'such property' in rule 100 as given in the above cases.

25. In the circumstances, the impugned order does not suffer from any error or illegality nor has resulted in failure of justice, we find seven years time too much for disposal of such summary proceedings, which nakedly exposes the sorry state of our judicial system.

26. In the result, both the Rules are discharged with costs. Order of stay granted at the time of issue of the Rules are hereby recalled and vacated. The executing Court is directed to take steps for expeditious restoration of possession to the claimants.

Communicate.

End.

lawyer:
Md Idrisur Rahman with Md Suza Al-Faruqu, Md Ekramul Islam Md Shahidullah and Pratikar Chakma, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners.
