full_judgment:
SK Sinha J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause why the judgment and decree dated 11-3-1999 of the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 231 of 1997 affirming those dated 21-4-1997 of the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 350 of 1995, should not be set aside.

2. The opposite parties instituted the suit seeking the following declarations:

(i) 	"For a decree declaring that the decision regarding fixation of valuation of the structure on the basis of 1989 PWD schedule mentioned in the allotment letter No. 150/93/6296 dated 28-8-93 is (sic) issued by the office defendant No. 4 is illegal, malafide and made without any lawful basis and has no legal effect and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

(ii) To pass necessary order or orders directing the defendants as per report of defendant No. 2 Chief Engineer, Housing and Settlement, Segun Bagicha, Dhaka vide Memo No. 3/344/1007 dated 7-5-92, also to make further direction to the defendants that in view of the plaintiff's social and financial status the defendants can realise the actual cost of the construction only from the plaintiff's i.e. Taka 24,535.77 (Taka twenty-four thousand five hundred thirty-five seventy-seven paisa) for each semi pucca tin shed house."

3. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that plaintiff No. 1 is Registered Society having registration No. Dha-02457 dated 31-7-90 under the name "Mirpur Semi Pucca (Tinshed) Basabaskari Kalayan Samity" and plaintiff No.2 is the President and plaintiff No. 3 is the Secretary of the said society in which 562 Members residing with their families in 562 Semi Pucca houses at Mirpur, who are mainly Government servants in various Ministries. After the independence of Bangladesh, some Semi-Pucca Tinshed houses were constructed for a period of 10 years by the official assistance of the Ministry of Rehabilitation in 1972. For proper accommodation of helpless persons, who were victims of the war of liberation as well as helpless Government servants who left Pakistan, the Government prepared a plan to accommodate Class III and Class IV employees at Sections I, II and VI, Mirpur, converting 1124 single tin sheds to 562 quarters. Allotment was made through defendant No. 2 fixing Taka 50 as rent per month for each quarter. Plaintiff No. 1 subsequently prayed for the Government on behalf of its members of the society for permanent lease of the said semi-pucca houses. In pursuance thereof a meeting was held on 12-9-90 by the members of plaintiff No. 1 society, which was presided over by the Minister, Ministry of Works, wherein it was decided that the aforesaid 562 houses would be leased out to the allotees on permanent basis. Accordingly, defendant No. 3 by Memo dated 22-2-90 informed defendant No. 1 to determine the valuation of the houses. The Executive Engineer accordingly assessed the construction cost of each house at Taka 24,537.77 and the price of per bigha of land at Taka 5.50 lac. The Executive Engineer again estimated the construction cost for each unit at Taka 1,32,368 as per the PWD schedule of 1989 and the price of the land at Taka 16 lac per bigha. There was no explanation as to why the construction cost of the houses was increased at Taka at 1, 32,368 in place of Taka 24,537.77. The houses were constructed in 1972 and they were in dilapidated conditions. Plaintiff No. 1 made a representation to the Ministry of Works on 26-12-93 raising objection against the fixation of the arbitrary valuation but the said appeal was rejected without giving any hearing to the plaintiffs. Thereafter plaintiff No. 1 again renewed its prayer but it was not entertained and ultimately the Assistant Commissioner, Housing and Settlement, defendant No.4, by letter dated 22-3-95 informed the plaintiffs that their appeal dated 26-12-93 and their application dated 11-7-94 could not be considered for administrative reasons. It has been stated in the plaint the alleged fixation of valuation of the structures in question by defendant No. 1 is arbitrary and malafide. The plaintiffs subsequently made repeated representations and were led to hope that justice would be done to them but they were informed by defendant No. 1 on 2-12-95 that the decision taken earlier cannot be changed and hence the suit.

4. Defendant Nos. 1-3 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all material allegations of the plaint and contended, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and manner and that the plaintiffs have no right, title, or interest over the suit property and, as such, they are not entitled to get the claimed reliefs. It is further case of the defendants that after the liberation of Bangladesh, in order to meet up acute residential problem of third and fourth class employees of the Government, the Government constructed 1124 semi-pucca tin shed houses in Mirpur section Nos. I, II and VI for accommodating them, which were eventually converted into 562 two-roomed tin shed houses and these were allotted to the Government's third class and fourth class employees at a monthly rent for some time but subsequently they stopped payment of monthly rent. Thereafter they applied to the Government for permanent lease. In accordance with the Government decision, defendant No. 3 asked defendant No. 1 on 22-9-90 to determine the valuation of the houses. The Chief Engineer, Dhaka Housing and Settlement, Mirpur Division No. 1, assessed the valuation of the structures separately on 7-5-92, fixing at Taka 1,62,368 per unit. Thereafter, the Ministry concerned on 9-2-93 decided to lease out the said houses on permanent basis on the terms and conditions, inter alia, that the persons who were occupying the houses since 1987 would get permanent lease; that the valuation of the land would be Taka 16 lac per bigha and the valuation of the structures of houses would be Taka 1,32,368 as per schedule 1989 of the Ministry of Works: that the allottees would pay the price of the land, structures and arrears of rent within 5 years by 10 installments: that on payment of the price as above, registered lease deeds would be executed after observing legal formalities and that the allottees having accepted the said terms, offer letters were issued to them.

5. The learned Subordinate Judge, on consideration of the evidence on record, decreed the suit and declared that the fixation of valuation of the structures in the allotment letter dated 22-8-93 is illegal and void. The learned Subordinate Judge directed defendant No. 2 to refuse the valuation of the structures of each house at Taka 24,537.77 following Memo No. 3/334/1007 dated 7-5-92.

6. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree, defendant No. 1 Government of Bangladesh preferred Title Appeal No. 231 of 1997, which was heard by the 1st Court, of Additional District Judge, Dhaka, who by his judgment dated 11-3-99 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

7. Mr Mihir Kanti Majumder, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the defendant-petitioner, submits that the plaintiffs have no Locus standi to maintain the suit, that the suit at the instance of the plaintiffs is not maintainable at all and that courts below having failed to consider those vital aspects of the case, illegally decreed the suit, which has occasioned failure of justice. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submits that regard being had to the fact that the suit was instituted challenging the fixation of valuation of the structures in the offer letter for permanent lease issued upon one Mr Md Mofizur Rahman, who has not challenged the said memo and he was not even impleaded in the suit and no offer letter having been made to the plaintiffs, the disputed offer letter does not affect any right or interest of the plaintiffs and, as such, the suit is not legally maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and therefore, the courts below clearly committed error of law in decreeing the suit. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submits that having regard to the admitted fact that the Government is the owner of the suit property and the plaintiffs have no vested right whatsoever, the plaintiffs are not entitled to get any decree as claimed in the suit but the courts below totally ignoring these vital questions decreed the suit irrelevant on illegal considerations and the same has occasioned failure of justice.

8. Mr Maksudur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties, on the other hand, submits that the fixation of valuation of structures in question as per 1989 schedule of the PWD is clearly illegal and arbitrary and, as such, the Courts below were fully justified in decreeing the suit on assigning cogent reasons. The learned Advocate further submits that the courts below having concurrently found that the fixation of price of the structures is arbitrary and that the defendants have failed to show any reasonable basis for such valuation, these concurrent findings of fact based on evidence cannot be disturbed by this court in exercise of revisional power. The learned Advocate further submits that plaintiff No. 1 being a registered co-operative society representing all the aggrieved 562 member allotees of semi-pucca houses, who were original lessees of the Government, the suit at the instance of the plaintiffs is legally maintainable.

9. In this case, the plaintiffs seek for a declaration- that the fixation of valuation of the structures of semi pucca houses in question as communicated under memo No. J-1-150/93/6296 dated 22-8-93 by the Commissioner of Settlement, Ministry of Works, is illegal, void, etc. and for a mandatory injunction directing the defendants to re-fix the valuation at Taka 24,537.77. The disputed memo was issued in favour of one Md Mofizur Rahman who is a lessee in a tin shed house, marked as Ext. 8. A close scrutiny of Ext. 8 shows that it was merely a letter of offer for lease of a semi pucca house for 99 years. The said allotment letter was issued asking lessee Md Mofizur Rahman to pay a sum of Taka 3,31,017, of which, Taka 46,649 was for arrears of rent, Taka 1,32,386 was for construction cost of tin shed house and Taka 1,52,000 as price of land, at a time or by instalments on the further stipulation that the first instalment was required to be paid within 30 days from the date of issuance of the letter and the balance amount of the price to be paid by six monthly instalments. It was further stipulated that in case of failure to make the first instalment within the given time, the allotment letter hall be treated as cancelled. It was specifically mentioned in the allotment letter that even after the registration of the lease deed on payment of the entire consideration, if it was found that the affidavit affirmed by the allottee was false, the Ministry of Works reserves the right to cancel the allotment on confiscating the money paid by him. It clearly mentioned that the allotment letter did not confer any right upon the allottee.

10. The allotment letter was issued on 22-8-92 and the suit was instituted on 22-11-95. There is no statement in the plaint or in the evidence that the said allottee has deposited the salami money or the first instalment within 30 days of issuance of the allotment letter. There is also no statement in the plaint that the defendants ever extended the time for payment of the first instalment. Clause 6 of the allotment letter clearly provides that in case of failure to fulfill Clause No. 4 i.e. failing to deposit the first instalment, the allotment letter shall stand cancelled. This clause is a self-executory clause. From this, we find that the allotment of the semi pucca house in favour of Md Mofizur Rahman stands cancelled before the date of institution of the suit. It further appears from Clause 11 thereof that the allottee shall acquire no right or title in the allotted house on the basis of the allotment letter Ext. 8. From this clause we find that the impugned allotment letter does not confer any right or interest in the semi-pucca house in favour of the allottee. On perusal of the clauses embodied in the disputed letter of allotment we find that no suit challenging the valuation of the structures fixed therein can be illegally maintainable, as the owner Government has the inalienable right to fix the value of the property to be leased out to intending lessees, who had no right to dictate terms of the lease and the value of the property. It is unfortunate that the Court below failed to address themselves to these moot questions involved in the suit and allowed them to be led by totally illegal and irrelevant consideration occasioning failure of justice.

11. To bring a suit seeking declaration under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, the plaintiffs must show that they have a legal character or any legal right to the property or that they have acquired any legal status in the subject-matter of the suit. No suit is maintainable unless the plaintiffs are person who are entitled to some legal character or to some right to the property in suit. Mere seeking a declaration in a suit of civil nature does not entitle the plaintiffs to such right or declaration as may be sought for, unless it is shown that they have any legal character or right in the subject-matter of the suit. Admittedly allottee Md Mofizur Rahman has not come to the Court to challenge the allotment letter issued to him. The plaintiffs claimed that though plaintiff No. 1 is not an allottee, yet it stands for all the allottees and members of the society and the plaintiffs have the locus standi to file the suit cannot be accepted on the simple reason that the samity itself is neither an allottee nor an aggrieved person because of the issuance of the disputed letter of allotment. We have already found that the allotment letter did not confer any right of title in the house in favour of the allottee. The learned Additional District Judge upon consideration of Ext, 3(b) came to the conclusion that" As no documents of contrary decision came from the custody of defendants hence I have nothing alternative to rely on the contents of the Exhibit 3(h) which is actually a paper preserved in the custody of the defendants. Hence fixing the price of the structure in question as per the schedule of 1989 of PWD was not appropriate and legal". We are of the view that this finding of the learned Additional District Judge is clearly vitiated by misreading of the material evidence and misconstruction of Exhibit 3(b).

12. In the plaint it has been stated that plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 are allottees who represent the other allottees. On perusal of the plaint, we find that the said 562 members of the society have not been impleaded in the suit either as plaintiffs or as defendants. Even we do not find in the record the names of the said 562 allottees, who formed the society under the name of plaintiff No. 1. The plaintiffs, in support of their claim, have filed a certificate issued by the Registrar, Social Welfare Department which has been marked as Exhibit 1. The said certificate does not show that plaintiff No. 1 Society was formed by 562 members, who were allottees of semi-pucca houses at Mirpur. In paragraph 22 of the plaint, it has been stated, that the plaintiffs instituted the suit in representative capacity. There is nothing on record to show that the plaintiffs filed the suit in representative capacity on fulfillment of conditions laid down for such a suit. To bring a suit in the representative capacity, the provisions of rule 8 of Order 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure have to be complied with. The rule provides as follows:

"8(1) Where there are numerous persons having the same interest in one suit, one or more of such persons may, with the permission of the Court, sue or be used, or may defend, in such suit, on behalf of or for the benefit of all persons so interested. But the Court shall in such case give, at the plaintiff's expense, notice of the institution of the suit to all such persons either by personal service or, where from the number of persons or any other cause such service is not reasonably practicable, by public advertisement, as the Court in each case may direct.

(2). Any person on whose behalf or for whose benefit a suit is instituted or defended under sub-rule (1) may apply to the Court to be made a party to such suit."

13. This Rule requires that the Court should exercise a judicial discretion permitting some definite persons to sue or be sued on behalf of all the persons interested. Leave of the Court has to be obtained under this Rule at the time of institution of the suit. The plaintiffs of courses can apply for such leave and to take such further action as required under the rule even during the pendency of the suit. In this suit, no leave under rule 8 of Order 1 was obtained by the plaintiff to sue on behalf of the 562 allotees; even no application was filed at any stage of the proceeding seeking permission of the Court to sue on their behalf.

<u>14. The object with which this provision was enacted is to facilitate decisions on questions in which a larger body of persons are interested without recourse to the ordinary procedure where each individual has to maintain action by separate suit. The principle is to prevent a defendant from being vexed or molested by other suits of similar nature. Rule 8 of Order 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that (a) all persons interested in the case be joined, (b) the relief is meant for the benefit and protection of other persons who have the same interest and (c) the suit be brought by following the procedures mentioned in the rule.</u>

<u>15. The essential conditions to be fulfilled in a suit of representative character are that the parties must be numerous, and there must be community of interest among them. This provision cannot be applied unless the plaintiffs truly represent the persons whom they seek to represent. A decree passed in a representative suit enures to the benefit of or binds all the persons represented in the suit. Where a suit is not representative, the decree cannot bind anyone, who is not a party to it. Plaintiffs though instituted the suit claiming as representatives of 562 allottees but they have challenged the allotment letter issued only to one Md Mofizur Rahman, who is not a party to the suit. In the absence of the necessary leave, the suit cannot assume the character of a representative suit. The suit is, therefore, not legally maintainable and is hit by Order 1 rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr Rahman, of course, submits that since plaintiff No. 1, being a registered society, representing 562 allottees, having instituted the suit on their behalf and the learned Subordinate Judge having adjudicated upon the suit, it may be presumed that the Court impliedly granted leave to the plaintiffs. This submission has no merit in view of the fact that no notice of the institution of the suit was issued to all the persons interested, whom the plaintiffs purport to represent, either by personal service or by public advertisement, which is the mandatory requirement of law.</u>

16. In support of the claim of the plaintiffs about arbitrary fixation of price, they have relied upon Exhibit 3 series, Exhibit 4, Exhibit 5 and Exhibit 11. Exhibit 3 series are letters between the Chief Engineer and the Executive Engineer of the Housing and Settlement Department relating to fixation of actual cost of the structures. Exhibit 4 series are the two appendices of letters or reports without the main letters to which they were appended, regarding fixation of valuation of the homestead of the displaced persons. These are loose sheets and the plaintiffs did not file the main letters or reports, which are incomplete documents relying upon which no decision can be arrived at as the said exhibits have practically no relevance with the impugned allotment letter, these being internal departmental correspondences for administrative purposes creating no right whatsoever for the plaintiffs. Exhibit 5 is a report submitted to the Ministry of Works from the Housing Department regarding fixation of price of the structures. Exhibit 11 is another letter which is not legible. No copy of these letters was communicated to the plaintiffs nor to Md Mofizur Rahman. All these letters are opinions and reports of inter-departmental correspondence made before finalisation of fixation of valuation of the structures in question, relying upon which, no conclusion can be arrived at that the valuation as mentioned in Exhibit 8 so far as it relates to the structures is arbitrary. These reports and opinions are also not legal evidence nor can they be used by the plaintiffs and the defendant Government. These reports and correspondences were made by public officers within the province of their normal administrative function, not amenable to judicial scrutiny. Such reports containing opinions of some public servants cannot give to plaintiffs any vested right in respect of the suit property and accordingly, these cannot be the basis for determination of the assumed rights on the plaintiff in judicial proceeding.

<u>17. In this case we have noticed that these documents are not legally eligible to be exhibited in the manner they have been exhibited on behalf of the plaintiffs. We have also noticed that at the time of exhibiting these documents, no objection was raised by the learned Government's Advocate and allowed the documents to be exhibited, even then, we are of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge should not have marked them as exhibits, as firstly, these documents are photo copies of the originals of which were not called for and secondly, these documents are confidential official letters beyond the access of the plaintiffs, the contents thereof are inadmissible evidence in the absence of originals. Despite the fact that no objection was raised at the time of marking these as exhibits, we are inclined to take exception in this particular case, because of the fact that these secret official documents are prima facie inadmissible in evidence in the absence of the original unless the formalities for acceptance of the documents were duly met. We are of the view that the courts below were manifestly wrong in marking these documents as exhibits in the case in a most casual fashion. Moreover, the settled law is that a document which is by itself not admissible in evidence cannot be made admissible simply because it has been marked as an exhibit. These documents, therefore, do not come to the assistance of the plaintiffs in proving their alleged right that really does not exist.</u>

<u>18. These exhibits are merely secondary evidence within the meaning of section 63(2) of the Evidence Act. The plaintiffs did not follow the minimum requirement of law in exhibiting the said documents and the learned Subordinate Judge has mechanically marked them exhibits. The fundamental rule must not be lost sight of the fact that the contents of document cannot be proved by secondary evidence unless a proper case is made out for its acceptance under sections 65 and 66 of the Evidence Act, which provide.</u>

<u>"65(a) when the original is shown or appears to be in the possession or power-</u>

<u>of the person against whom the document is sought to be proved, or of any person out of reach of, or not subject to, the process of the Court, or of any person legally bound to produce it, and when, after the notice mentioned in section 66, such person does not produce it;</u>

<u>(b) 	.</u>

<u>(c) 	.</u>

<u>(d) 	.</u>

<u>(e) 	.</u>

<u>"66. Secondary evidence of the contents of the documents referred to in section 65, clause (a), shall not be given unless the party proposing to give such secondary evidence has previously given to the party in whose possession or power the document is, or to his Advocate such no notice to produce it as is prescribed by law, and if no notice is prescribed by law, then such notice as the court considers reasonable under the circumstances of the case."</u>

<u>Secondary evidence of documents mentioned in section 65(a) may be given if the procedure laid down in section 66 is strictly complied with. Before the reception of secondary evidence, it must be proved that the documents were in possession of a person against whom it has been sought to be proved and such person though noticed has failed to produce it.</u>

<u>19. From the order sheet of the suit, we find that the plaintiffs did not file any application for directing the defendants for producing the originals of the documents sought to be exhibited in the suit. The plaintiffs sole witness did not state in his evidence that he prayed for said documents. Even he did not explain as to how he procured the copies of the documents from the offices of the defendants. Unless and until necessary formalities are complied with, secondary evidence will be inadmissible. Therefore, the acceptance of the secondary evidence by the Subordinate Judge and his decision in the suit relying upon such non-admissible evidence are errors of law apparent on the face of the record.</u>

20. The learned Deputy Attorney-General has taken us to the written statement and submits that the defendant Government has seriously challenged the maintainability of the suit. The learned Subordinate Judge though framed an issue about the maintainability of the suit, yet he did not give any decision thereon, although he noticed that the Government has challenged the suit on the ground of maintainability. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submits that the learned Additional District Judge also formulated a point in that regard but did not decide the point and evasively held that "as the opportunity of paying the ad valorem court fee has not yet been exhausted, hence the suit is maintainable". The learned Additional District Judge was totally unmindful of the main issue involved in the suit, and held that Civil Court has jurisdiction to try the suit, which is not at all an issue in the suit. Therefore, we are of the view that the decision of the learned Additional District Judge that the suit is maintainable is based upon superficial consideration of the materials on record and the same has resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

21. We are shocked to note that the learned Additional District Judge as well as the learned Subordinate Judge without considering the question of maintainability of the suit, which goes at the root of the matter at issue to be adjudicated upon, decreed the suit on a superficial consideration of the materials on record. If on a mere reading of the plaint it is found that the suit is not maintainable, the Court is required, to decide the said issue before deciding other issues involved in the suit. In this suit, both the Courts below failed to address themselves to this vital issue in an effective and meaningful manner. We are, therefore, of the opinion that the decisions of the Courts below, which are based upon such non-consideration of vital points, are not sustainable in law.

22. As regards the submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite parties that even if it is found that the findings of the Learned Courts below are errors apparent on the face of the record, no interference under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is called for by this Court unless it is shown that these are vitiated by misreading or non-consideration of material evidence on record, has merits and consideration in view of the fact that the learned Subordinate Judge has declared the impugned Memo at the instance of the plaintiffs who have no locus standi to seek such declaration and that the plaintiffs are not legally entitled to the reliefs as prayed for in the suit.

23. For the reasons stated above, we find substance in this Rule and the judgments and decrees of the Courts below are required to be interfered with. The Rule is, therefore, made absolute with costs. The judgment and decree dated 11-3-99 of the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 231 of 1997 affirming those dated 21-4-97 of the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 350 of 1995 are hereby set aside. The suit stands dismissed.

Let a copy of the judgment be communicated to Mr Md Nurul Islam then Subordinate Judge, Dhaka by name at his present assignment for his perusal and future guidance.

End.

Gouri Das and ors ----- Appellants 
Vs.
ABM Hasan Kabir and others  ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 15-1-1995 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos. 2407 & 7793 of 1991).
full_judgment:
K.M. Hasan, J: These two appeals by special leave are directed against the judgment and order of the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos. 2407 and 7793 of 1991 dated 15-1-1995 making the Rules absolute in the former and discharging the Rule in the latter.

2. These appeals arose out of two title suits being Title Suit No. 171 of 1985 and Title Suit No. 133 of 1981.

3. The Title Suit No. 171 of 1985 was filed by the respondent, ABM Hasan Kabir as plaintiff impleading predecessor-in-interest of the defendant appellants and others for a declaration of title and recovery of khas possession.

4. Haripada Das, predecessor of the defendant appellants as a plaintiff, filed Title Suit No. 133 of 1981 impleading Ava Rani Aich, ABM Hasan Kabir and other defendants for a declaration of title and recovery of khas possession.

5. There was a third Title Suit being Title Suit No. 303 of 1980 renumbered as Title Suit No. 172 of 1985 filed by the respondent ABM Hasan Kabir challenging the order of the Chairman of the Municipal Committee treating the holding as enemy property.

6. All the aforesaid three suits were tried together and dismissed by a common judgment by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Comilla by judgment dated 2-11-1988.

7. Against Title Suit No. 171 of 1985, Title Appeal No. 260 of 1988 was filed and against Title Suit No. 133 of 1981, Title Appeal No. 20 of 1999 was filed. Both the appeals were heard together and dismissed by the District Judge, Comilla affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court by his judgment dated 18-3-1991. Against Title Suit No. 172 of 1985 no appeal was preferred.

8. The plaintiff respondent's case in Title Suit No. 171 of 1985 is that, the property mentioned in the schedule 1 of the plaint originally belonged to three brothers, namely, Mahim Chandra Aich, Satish Chandra Aich and Opendra Chandra Aich who became owners of the same on the basis of a kabuliyat dated 31st Baishak, 1332 BS. Thereafter, by amicable partition between themselves Mahim Chandra Aich got the land mentioned in the schedule 1 of the plaint and was in exclusive possession of the property for more than 50 years by constructing building and huts thereon. Mahim Chandra Aich died leaving his only son, Binayendra Aich who was also in actual physical possession of the suit property for more than 12 years. He died leaving behind his wife Ava Rani Aich and two sons, namely, Dharanindra Aich and Bijoy Krishna Aich. Bijoy Krishna relinquished his claim in his paternal property. Thus Ava Rani Aich and Dharanindra Aich remained in possession of the suit property of late Binayendra Aich in assertion of their right, title and possession thereon. The record of right was finally published in the name of their heirs. They sold the suit land by registered kabala dated 31-1-1972 to the plaintiff-respondent No.1, ABM Hasan Kabir who went into possession of the first schedule property of the plaint along with other suit properties which was under possession of the defendant appellants as monthly tenants. The defendant appellants agreed to pay monthly rent to the plaintiff. Thereafter, on demand of the rent, the defendant appellants refused to pay rent and finally on 2-11-1981 denied the right, title and interest of the plaintiff in respect of the suit property. Hence, the Title Suit No. 171 of 1985 was initiated.

9. The defendant appellants contested the suit by filing written statement denying all material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that they were never monthly tenants under the plaintiff-respondent or his vendor. They claimed that they were tenants under Hari Prasad Das to whom they have been paying rent since 1972. Hari Prasad Das took settlement of the suit land from Binayendra in the year 1940 and possessing the same on payment of ground rent as non-agricultural tenant. Hari Prasad was still residing in the suit property with his family members. Binayendra was never in possession of the suit land and after his death, his sons and wife never inherited the suit property and by mistake in RS khatian name of Ava Rani Aich was recorded with respect to the suit land. It is also claimed that the defendant-appellants never paid any rent to the vendor of the plaintiff-respondent and they never promised to pay rent to the plaintiff-respondent after the latter claimed to have purchased the suit land and the plaintiff-respondent never demanded any rent from the defendant-appellants So, the plaintiff-respondent has got no right, title and possession of the suit land.

10. The defendant-appellants landlord, Hari Prasad Das, earlier filed Title Suit No. 133 of 1981 for declaration of title on the basis of settlement in the same suit property, described in schedule 1, claiming that his father Baroda Prasad Das took settlement of the land from Binoyendra Aich in 1940 and constructed huts thereon and possessed the same by residing in some huts and letting out others to monthly tenants. After the death of Baroda Prosad Das, he had possessed the suit property for more than the statutory period of limitation and acquired an indefeasible non- agricultural tenancy right.

11. The Government as defendant in Title Suit Nos. 171 of 1985 and 133 of 1981 appeared and claimed that the suit property had vested as an enemy property.

12. Title Suit No. 172 of 1985 was filed by AB Hasan for declaration that the creation of a municipal holding in the name of Hari Prasad in respect of six huts standing in the suit land was illegal.

13. The trial Court after hearing three suits analogously dismissed the suits and also held that the suit property was not an enemy property. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the trial Court both the plaintiffs in the aforementioned suits filed title appeal before the District Judge, Comilla being Title Appeal Nos. 260 of 1988 and 20 of 1989 which were heard analogously and dismissed by the judgment and decree dated 18-3- 1991. Against which Civil Revision Nos. 2407 and 7793 of 1991 were preferred before the High Court Division. Rules were obtained and finally a Single Judge of the High Court Division made the Rule absolute in Civil Revision No. 2407 of 1991, but discharged the Rule in Civil Revision No. 7793 of 1991 by his judgment dated 15-1-1995.

14. Being aggrieved the defendant- appellants sought leave to appeal before this Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 318 of 1995 and 341 of 1995. Leave was granted to consider the following:

"The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred in failing to consider and decide the specific case of the petitioners as to acquisition of non-agricultural tenancy right in the suit property by possession for more than the statutory period upon erecting huts and residing therein, after taking settlement from the admitted owner Binayendra Aich in 1940. In view of the findings of the courts below as to the petitioner's continued possession from the time of their predecessor-in-interest, Had Prasad Das and the law contained in section 7 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. High Court Division erred in making the Rule in Civil Revision No. 2407 of 1991 absolute and in discharging the Rule in Civil Revision No. 7793 of 1991 without any finding on the petitioner's case of title. Lastly, the courts below having found long possession of the petitioners, presumption should be in their favour as to the lawful character of such possession, unless the contrary is proved and holding such possession to be proof of settlement by the admitted owner Binayendra Aich in favour of Hari Prasad Das in 1940 as claimed by the petitioner."

15. From the above, it may be drawn that the defendant-appellant's claim is based on three legal presumptions as for example, permanency of tenancy, adverse possession and lastly, the long possession.

16. The facts and circumstances of each case will determine whether the presumption of permanency of tenancy should be made or not. In respect of non-agricultural tenancy holding created before the Transfer of Property Act the existence of the following elements are necessary in order to make out the presumption of permanency of tenancy.

(1) The origin of a tenancy for residential purpose must be unknown and the principle of a lost grant is invoked by tenant.

(2) Existence of a permanent pucca building on the lands built long before the arising of any controversy and that to the knowledge of the landlord.

(3) Regular payment of rent.

(4) Reorganisation of succession and transfer by the landlord.

17. The first two are essential elements and their absence will be ordinarily fatal to any claim of permanency of tenancy. But the absence of third and fourth elements usually will raise difficulties in the way of raising the presumption, but may not be decisive if there are other circumstances in aid of the presumption.

18. The defendant-appellants' claim that their landlord Hari Prasad Das's father Baroda Prasad Das took settlement from BinoyendraAich in 1940 and, as such, it cannot be said that the origin of their tenancy for residential purpose was unknown. But, in fact, they could not produce any paper in support of their claim. Further, they do not claim to have constructed any permanent structure on the land to the knowledge of Baroda Prasad Das, from whom they took the settlement. On the other hand, they claim that Baroda Prasad Das erected twelve huts in plot No. 947 and used to reside in some huts with his family and used to possess the other huts through monthly tenants. Upon these facts no substantial findings can be made out that any pucca building on the land was built to the knowledge of the landlord to justify the presumption of permanency of tenancy. The defendant-appellants also claim that the Municipal holding was also created in his father's name and he has been paying municipal taxes regularly. Admittedly, all the courts have found them in possession but they could not produce any patta kabuliyat in support of the alleged settlement in favour of Baroda Prasad Das from Binoyendra Aich in the year 1940. Three typed receipts have been marked as exhibit I series in Title Suit No. 133 of 1981 to prove the payment of ground taxes to Binayendra Aich. In these receipts it is mentioned that Rs. 60.00 was received by Binayendra Aich in respect of ground tax and municipal holding Nos. 185, 186 and 152(a) of Bazrapur Mohalla of Comilla Town. All the courts below held that from these receipts it could not be said that Baroda Prasad took settlement of the said land from Binayendra Aich. We do not also find any reason to disagree with them. Thus the defendant appellants failed to establish uniform payment of rent raising difficulties in the way of presumption of permanency of tenancy.

<u>19. Mr Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel, referred to section 7(2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, to advance his argument of adverse possession. Under the section a tenant must show that he had been holding the property in question for a period of not less than twelve years without any lease. Mere suggestion of uninterrupted possession for "12 years" or that the plaintiff had acquired "an absolute title" is not enough to raise such a plea. (1) To claim adverse possession it must be specifically pleaded in the plaint, (2) hostile title must be asserted, (3) adverse possession must be adequate in continuity, (4) Evidence must be adduced to show when possession became adverse so that the starting point of limitation against the party affected can be found. But in the instant case' there was no attempt to prove since when the adverse possession has started. There is no evidence here when possession became adverse as long possession is not necessarily adverse possession.</u>

<u>20. Lastly, Mr Khandkar Mahbubuddin, has relied on 29 CWN 138, 128 and 43 CWN 828 to show that if a person is in possession of a land for a very long time, there is a presumption in his favour under section 110 of the Evidence Act. There is no dispute as to the proposition of law. But we are to see whether the facts upon which reliance has been placed unequivocally point to long possession by the defendant appellants of the suit property. The presumption under section 110 in this case would apply only if two conditions are satisfied viz, that the possession of the person claiming long possession is not prima facie wrongful and secondly, the title of the person, in this case the plaintiff-respondent, against whom the long possession is claimed is not proved. The courts below found that the defendant-appellants are in possession but they could not prove their title or that they are not in possession to the knowledge of the real owner upon denying his title or any kabuliyat or deed of settlement. On the other hand, the plaintiff-respondent has proved their title by registered kabala executed on 13-11-1978 for valuable consideration. This kabala has not been disbelieved by the courts below. This hits at the root of the claim by the defendant- appellants on the suit land on the basis of long possession since their claim of title of the suit property has been disbelieved by the courts below. No doubt the defendant-appellants' possession for a long time and by succession are material. But the claim of long possession remains precarious because of the finding of title of the suit land in favour of the plaintiff- respondent by courts below.</u>

21. Before concluding we want to observe that the inference of permissive possession by the High Court Division is not correct inference.

In view of the above, the appeals are dismissed without any order as to cost.

End.

parties:
Government of Bangladesh, represented by Secretary, Housing and Settlement Bangladesh Secretariat & others  ------ Petitioners 
Vs.
ASM Firojuddin Bhuiyan  ------ Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
A judgment of reversal has been called in question by petitioner in invoking this Court's Civil Revisional Jurisdiction on laying a petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure whereupon a Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why judgment and decree dated 26-1-1998 passed by learned Additional District Judge. Second Court. Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 136 of 1997 setting aside judgment and decree dated 29-5-1997 passed by learned Assistant Judge, First Court. Dhaka in Title Suit No. 368 of 1985 should not be set aside.

2. The only question that survives for determination in this Civil Revision Petition is whether the principle of promissory estoppel is attracted in awarding a decree in favour of petitioner.

3. For the purpose of answering the said question posed portrayal of essential facts may conveniently be noticed and stated.

4. Petitioner of Civil Revision Petition as plaintiff on 17-8-1985 laid a suit being Title Suit No. 368 of 1985 in the First Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge). Dhaka for a decree that defendants are legally bound to execute necessary documents relating to the suit property in favour of plaintiff after accepting the price fixed by Government and also for a decree that sale of suit property by auction or otherwise to any outsider other than plaintiff is illegal and also for a further decree that the auction schedule to be held on July 31, 1985 or, thereafter, is highly illegal. The Secretary Ministry of Works, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others had been impleaded as defendants. Averments made in the plaint were that the plaintiff took rent of the suit property from one Md Amin from January, 1968 and had been in occupation of the suit property on carrying on business under the name and style Messers General Exporters and had been using the suit property for residential purpose. Rent of the suit premises was fixed at Taka 90 per month and plaintiff continued payment of rent upto the month of February 1972. Plaintiff failed to trace out the landlord after the month of February, 1972 and applied to Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar (South) Dhaka for declaring the suit property as abandoned property within the meaning of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 Ministry of Works declared the suit property as abandoned property on 20-3-1975 and demanded arrear rent from 1-1-1977 at the rate of Taka 314 per month, in total Taka 11,932 Plaintiff paid rent as demanded and continued paying rent regularly.

5. Further pleading is that Ministry of Works by letter dated 30-12-1975 informed plaintiff that in view of public utility Government decided to hold the suit property and requested plaintiff to hand over possession of the same in favour of Executive Engineer, City Building Division. PWD within 30 days of the receipt of letter, Plaintiff thereafter, requested Government for reconsideration of its decision. Government at the request of plaintiff reconsidered its decision and allowed plaintiff to continue his business by letter dated 9-9-1976. Plaintiff had been continuing his business on the suit property. Government, thereafter, enhanced rent of suit premises from Taka 314 to 1645 per month from 4-9-1983. Plaintiff also paid enhanced rent: Government on 4-9-1983 decided to sell the abandoned houses to lawful allottees. The decision was published through national newspapers and Government constituted a Valuation Committee. Valuation Committee valued the suit premises after enquiry and recommended to transfer suit property to plaintiff at the valuation decided by the committee. Sub-Divisional Engineer, defendant No.6, by his letter dated 6-8-1984 informed defendant No.5 Executive Engineer, PWD that the Valuation Committee determined valuation of suit property. Plaintiff expressed his willingness to deposit money as per valuation determined by Valuation Committee. Plaintiff was advised by defendant No.3. Section Officer, Ministry of Works to keep fund available for depositing required money when called for. In spite of repeated requests by plaintiff the defendants did not allow plaintiff to deposit money. Plaintiff had been enjoying suit property in compliance with all legal formalities including regular payment of rent in favour of Government. Plaintiff to his utter surprise received a letter dated 13-7-1985 from defendant No. 3 informing that Government had taken decision to sell the suit premises within 10 (ten) days.

6. The positive assertion put forward by plaintiff is that since plaintiff remained in possession and occupation of suit premises for more than 18 years and since he accepted the offer to purchase the suit property as per valuation determined by Abandoned Authority a right had been created in his favour which could not be taken away by malafide action of defendants. Plaintiff further pleaded that the suit property if sold in auction, the loss and damage and the misery of plaintiff would be extreme and that could not be compensated. Further stand taken is that defendants got no legal right to put the suit property to auction as plaintiff having continuous possession of the suit property for more than 18 years and he was always ready to purchase the suit property on value determined by valuation committee and still now agreed to pay the same.

7. Defendants resisted the suit on presentation of a written statement with contentions that the suit property was admittedly an abandoned property within the meaning of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and had been under the control and management, supervision of the defendants through allottee ASM Firoj Uddin Bhuiyan. The suit property is a commercial unit. Plaintiff got no legal right to proceed with the suit against Government. Defendants reserved their right to dispose of the suit property in any manner they liked. Defendant had been given a right to participate in the suit property through tender.

8. Over the above pleadings the parties fought out the suit.

9. Evidence, both oral and documentary, had been led in support of respective contentions. Plaintiff examined himself in support of his case. Defendants did not produce any witness in support of their case.

10. Learned Senior Assistant Judge, First Court, Dhaka by judgment and decree dated 29-5-1997 dismissed the suit In recording dismissal the learned Senior Assistant Judge as the trial Judge held that it was not proved that plaintiff was the allotted person on suit property and plaintiff got title on the basis of allotment and possession and title of plaintiff on the suit property was not proved. Learned Senior Assistant Judge then took the view that the plaintiff was required to prove possession over a period of 60 years in order to get decree of acquisition of title by adverse possession against Government and, as such, the plaintiff is not entitled to have a decree. Learned Senior Assistant Judge also took the view that plaintiff did not lay any suit for Specific Performance of Contract and did not pay ad valorem Court fee on the valuation of the suit and without institution of a suit for Specific Performance of Contract and without proving the contract plaintiffs suit was not at all maintainable. Learned Senior Assistant Judge, thereafter, found that plaintiff got no locus standi to institute the suit. In conclusion learned Senior Assistant Judge recorded decision that there was no ground on the part of plaintiff to seek reliefs as prayed by him.

11. Plaintiff felt aggrieved of the above adjudication and sought setting aside through a medium of appeal being Title Appeal No. 136 of 1997 before learned District Judge, Dhaka. Learned Additional District Judge, Second Court, Dhaka heard the appeal and by judgment and decree dated 26-1-1998 allowed it, set aside the judgment and decree recorded by trial judge and decreed plaintiffs suit and directed defendant-Government to register a document on acceptance of valuation fixed by Government and also declared sale by auction of the suit property to any stranger to be illegal. Learned appellate Judge discussed and considered evidences both oral and documentary and also fact and circumstances of the case, and found that since 1968 plaintiff as a tenant resided on the suit property and carried on business thereon and he was paying rents regularly. Learned appellate Judge also found that the valuation committee fixed Taka 7,27,410 as the valuation of the suit property and recommended to sell the same in favour of plaintiff. Appellate Judge recorded decision that plaintiff through legal evidence could prove his case and defendants did not at all prove their case on production of any witness in support of their case

12. Feeling aggrieved by the decision rendered by learned appellate Judge the defendants as petitioners approached this Court in this Civil Revision Petition and obtained this Rule.

13. Mr Bhivash Chandra Biswas, learned Assistant Attorney-General appeared for the petitioners. Opposite party is represented by Mr Md Nurul Huq with Mr AKM Shahidul Huq, Ms Tania Siddiqua and Ms Chamon Akhter, learned Advocates.

14. Contention pressed into service from the side of defendants petitioners is that the plaintiff got no status or character to challenge the decision of the Government in the matter of putting the suit property to auction and plaintiff having been an allottee under defendant-Government was bound by decision taken by it.

<u>15. Repelling, the said contention it is pressed from the side of plaintiff-opposite-party that the plaintiff-opposite party had been living on the suit property since 1968 and said matter was considered by Government and on considering plaintiff as an allottee he was directed to deposit rent fixed by Government and opposite party already deposited the said rent and. as such, he was entitled to get the property transferred in his name on payment of Taka 7,27,410 fixed by valuation committee and defendant-Government stood debarred under promissory estoppel from doing otherwise. Reliance had been placed upon some authorities notably amongst others are Messers Motilal Padanipat Sligar Mills Co Ltd is The State of Uttar Pradesh and others AIR 1979 (SC) 621Century Spinning & Manufacturing Co Ltd and another vs The Ulhasnagar Municipal Council and another AIR 1971 (SC) 1021: SP (Supendra Prashad) Misra vs Oil & Natural Gas Commission AIR 1987 1 Cal=90 CWN 449 and Robertson vs Minister of Pensions 1 KB 227 (LR) Kings Bench Division for the submission pressed.</u>

16. In approaching the controversy, section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the Doctrine of Promissory Estoppel embodied in section 115 of the Evidence Act may profitably be noticed.

17. Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act enjoins that any person entitled to any legal character or to any right as to any property may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right and the Court may in its discretion make therein a declaration that he is so entitled and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief. Provision states that no Court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title omits to do so.

18. Section 42 does not postulate all types of declarations but only a declaration that the plaintiff its "entitled to legal character or to any right as to any property and it warrants this kind of relief only under certain special circumstances. Relief enshrined under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is a discretionary relief and the said discretion is to be exercised on sound judicial principles.

<u>19. Promissory Estoppel is a principle evolved by Courts on the principles of equity and to avoid injustice. Where one party by his words and conduct make the other party a clear promise that promise would be binding upon the former who would not be entitled to go back from it.</u>

20. "Estoppel" in Black's Law Dictionary is indicated to mean that a party is prevented by his own acts from claiming a right to the detriment of other party who was entitled to rely on such conduct and has acted accordingly. Section 115 of the Evidence Act is also more or less couched in a language which conveys the same expression.

21. "Promissory Estoppel" is defined as in Black's Law Dictionary as that which arises when there is a promise which promissor should reasonably expect to induce action or forbearance of a definite and substantial character on the part of promise and which does induce such action or forbearance and such promise is binding if injustice can be avoided only by enforcement of promise".

<u>22. Lord Denning in Central London Property Trust Ltd vs High Trees House Ltd 1947 QB 130 stated as under:</u>

<u>"A promise intended to be binding intended to be acted upon, and, in fact, acted upon is binding."</u>

23. Admittedly, plaintiff-petitioner had been and has been living on the suit property since the year 1968. The suit property having been declared as Abandoned Property, the Government accepted plaintiff-petitioner as an allottee and he was directed to deposit arrear rents fixed by Government since the year 1972 and plaintiff-opposite-party already deposited the said rents. Taka 7,27,410 had been fixed as valuation of the suit property and plaintiff was willing to purchase the property on depositing the said amount of Taka 7,27,410.

24. Plaintiff as PW 1 gave testimony in support of plaintiffs case. He produced documents in support of his claim, Exhibit-I is a letter issued from section officer, Ministry of Works, Urban Development. PWD dated 20-3-1975 evidencing that plaintiff was directed to pay arrear rents at the rate of Taka 314 per month from 1-1-1972 to 28-2- 1973 amounting to Taka 11.932. Exhibit-5 are duplicate challans manifesting payment of monthly rent for the abandoned house at Taka 314 for the month of January and February, 1980. Exhibit-a is the valuation statement by Five (5) Member Committee appointed by Ministry of Works fixing Taka 7,27,410. Exhibit-5 series (21 challans) starting from 30-1-1975 to 30-3-1984 manifested payment of monthly rent by plaintiff to defendant-Government. Exhibit-7 is a letter issued from Ministry of Works dated 3-6-1984 to plaintiff noting the decision that the portion in occupation of ASM Firoj Uddin Bhuiyan plaintiff would be sold to him on the valuation determined by Government.

25. From all the documents it became evidently clear that plaintiff remained in possession over suit property since the year 1968 first as a tenant under Md Amin and then under the Government as an allottee and plaintiff paid rents to Government including all arrear rents and Government also took decision that the suit property would be sold to plaintiff on the price fixed by it. Equity and natural justice demand that plaintiff is not to be deprived of the suit property. Government, thus, is very much bound by its promise to sell the property in favour of plaintiff and it cannot now fall back and also cannot say that the suit property would be put to auction.

26. It is canvassed from the side of defendant-petitioner that plaintiff-opposite party could very much participate in the auction and could purchase the suit property through auction. The contention may be attractive but carries no substance. It is not understood why plaintiff would go for participating in auction to purchase suit property in view of the promise given by Government to plaintiff to sell the property on the valuation fixed by valuation committee constituted by Government.

<u>27. From the above discussion inevitable conclusion that flows is that on the strength of the Doctrine of Promissory Estoppel defendant Government is under a legal duty to execute a document of title with respect to suit property on acceptance of the price fixed by valuation committee constituted by defendant Government and the selling of suit property by auction to anybody else otherwise than plaintiff is illegal.</u>

28. Coming now to the propriety and legality of decisions reached by Courts below it appears that the approach of trial judge in dismissing the suit does not appear to be a correct approach and the reasoning adopted by learned trial judge is unintelligible. Admittedly plaintiff was in possession and occupation of the suit property and Government accepted him as an allottee on accepting rent from him.

29. Learned trial judge thus committed a patent illegality in finding that the possession of plaintiff over the suit property was not proved. Plaintiff did not claim any title over the suit property rather he claimed to have a deed of sale executed and registered by Government in his favour. The finding of learned trial judge to the effect that the plaintiff was required to prove his possession for a period exceeding 60 years otherwise he would not get any declaration of title by way of adverse possession is purely wooden and the process of reasoning adopted by the trial judge is unsustainable inasmuch as plaintiff did not claim acquisition of the title by adverse possession and the finding on this aspect of the matter is absolutely perverse. Learned trial judge also committed a grave error in finding that plaintiff got no ground to seek relief that Government was not entitled to sell out the suit property to any other else except plaintiff and also, that there was no justification for declaring auction illegal.

30. This brings me now to the soundness of decisions rendered by the appellate judge. Appellate Judge discussed and considered the evidence of plaintiff both oral and documentary and took into account oral testimony of plaintiff as PW 1 and held that plaintiff could prove his case through competent witnesses. Appellate Judge also found that defendants did not make any endeavour to prove their case on production of witnesses. The decision, reasons and conclusion reached by the appellate judge appear to be well founded on law and rooted in evidencing both oral and documentary backed by materials brought on record and those do not suffer from any patent illegality, legal infirmity, perversity and flagrant error' of law warranting any interference by this Court in the exercise of Civil Revisional Jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

31. No interference is, therefore, called for.

32. Resultantly, the Rule arising out of Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure stands discharged, however, without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree recorded by the learned Additional District Judge, Second Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 136 of 1997 are maintained.

Lower Courts Record be sent as immediate as possible.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was obtained by the (decree-holders) defendants upon making a revision application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against order No. 87 dated 10-5-2000 passed by Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Bogra in Other Class Suit No. 78 of 1987 by which their prayer for vacating stay was refused.

2. It is stated that on 25-9-85 the petitioners instituted Other Class Suit No. 181 of 1985 in the Court of Munsif, First Court at Bogra for eviction of the predecessor-in-interest of the opposite parties, Ismail Sheikh as a licensee. Suit was decreed ex parte on 2-2-86. On 24-4-86 said Ismail Sheikh died leaving the opposite parties as his heirs and legal representatives. Before his death, he unsuccessfully moved an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code being Miscellaneous Case No. 103 for setting aside the ex parte decrees which was alternately withdrawn, Opposite parties then preferred an appeal against the ex parte decree being Other Class Appeal No. 143 of 1987 which was allowed on 22-9-93 and the case was sent back on remand to the trial Court for fresh trial. Against that order of remand the petitioners obtained a Rule in Civil Revision No. 747 of 1994 and this Division by its order dated 6-1-98 made the Rule absolute and set aside the orders of remand.

3. On 25-3-87 opposite parties also instituted Other Class Suit No. 78 of 1985 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge at Bogra for declaration of title and also for declaring the ex parte decree dated 2-2-86 as null and void. The suit was then re-numbered as Other Suit No. 78 of 1987.

4. In the meantime, the petitioners started Execution Case No. 10 of 1986 for possession. Opposite Parties made an application under Order 21 rule 29 of the Code for stay before the executing Court and the executing Court by its order dated 26-7-98 rejected the prayer. Against that order opposite parties unsuccessfully moved a revision application being Civil order No. 3622 of 1998 which was summarily rejected. Civil petition being No. 113 of 1998 made before the Appellate Division therefrom was also dismissed on 3-12-98. The opposite parties again moved an application for stay of the further proceedings of the execution before the executing Court till disposal of their Other Class Suit No. 78 of 1987. Hearing the application, the executing court by its order dated 2-3-99 rejected the application. Against that order the opposite parties moved this Division again and obtained a Rule in Civil Revision No. 890 of 1999 and the Civil Revision was heard on 2-3-2000 and the Rule was discharged by this Division.

5. Then, the petitioners again went to the executing court for possession and the opposite parties made an application discussing for the first time that the Subordinate Judges has already stayed further proceeding of the execution case by order dated 16-3-2000 till disposal of Other Class Suit No. 78 of 1987 Then the petitioners on 17-4-2000 made an application before the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Bogra in other Class Suit No, 78 of 1987 for vacating the order of stay dated 16-3-98. Hearing the application and the objection of opposite parties thereto dated  27-4-2000 learned Subordinate Judge rejected the prayer and maintained the earlier order of stay granted by him by the impugned order.

6. Mr Md Muzaffar Hossain, learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the Subordinate Judge acted beyond his jurisdiction in staying further proceedings of the execution case pending before the executing court which has resulted in serious miscarriage of justice. He also cites the decision in the case of Alhaj Mirza Shamsuddin Beg vs Bangladesh and another reported in 41 DLR 356 where it has been held that the principle of constructive res judicata applies here on the defence now taken by the respondent corporation is hit by principle of estoppel by judgment The Corporation will be estopped from raising those defences which were taken by them in the previous proceedings and which was decided against them conclusively and finally.

7. Mr Md Mansur Habib, learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party, first read out the provisions of Order 21 rule 29 of the Code of Civil Procedure and submits that in view of such provision any court other than the executing court can stay further proceedings of any executing case if other conditions of the Rule are satisfied.

<u>8. I read again the provision of rule 29 of Order 21 of the Code. It says "where a suit is pending in any court against the holder of a decree of such court, on the part of the person against whom the decree was passed, the court may, on such terms as to security or otherwise as it thinks fit, stay execution of the decree until the pending suit has been decided." This power has been clearly given to an Executing Court as well as to the court in which suit impeaching the decree is pending if the decree is a decree of this court. In the case of Sunahar Ali vs Mohammed Akuali, reported in PLD 1957 Dhaka, 603 it was so decided. The decree in question was passed by Munsif, First Court, Bogra and, as such, the Subordinate Judge, First Court, at Bogra in which the suit is now pending cannot be deemed to be such court under the Rule to have jurisdiction to stay further proceedings of Execution Case No. 10 of 1986 of the above court of Senior Assistant Judge, Moreover, the discretion exercised twice by the executing court at the instance of the judgment-debtors in refusing to grant stay of execution was found to be valid up to the Appellate Division. The Subordinate Judge in proceeding with the title Suit is also not the court within the meaning of Order 21 rule 29 of the Code. Therefore, learned Subordinate Judge acted beyond his jurisdiction in granting stay of further proceeding of the execution case No. 10 of 1986 pending before the Senior Assistant Judge, 1st Court at Bogra. In the circumstances, the learned Subordinate Judge committed serious error of law in not vacating such an order of stay when it was so prayed for by the petitioners in their application dated 17-4-2000 which has resulted in serious miscarriage of justice.</u>

9. Further submission of Mr Mansur Habib is that before learned Subordinate Judge no objection was raised as to exercise of jurisdiction nor in the present Civil Revision any such plea was taken by the petitioners. Such omission of the petitioners, if any, does not deprive this Division to see whether order of stay was passed in lawful exercise of jurisdiction or not and or whether the impugned order refusing to vacate such order of stay is sanctioned by law or not. Submission of Mr Mansur Habib has no substance.

In the result, this Rule is made absolute. No order as to costs. The impugned order dated 10-5- 2000 passed by the Subordinate, Judge, 1st Court, Bogra in Other Class Suit No. 78 of 1987 refusing to vacate order of stay dated 16-3-98 staying further proceedings of the execution case No. 10 of 1986 of the Court of Senior Assistant Judge 1st Court at Bogra till disposal of the suit is set aside. The execution Court is directed to proceed with the execution of Execution Case No. 10 of 1986 as usual according to law, Communicate this order at once.

End.
