parties:
Abdul Jalil Molla ------ Petitioner
vs
Sree Mati Dasi and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment: This Rule at the instance of the judgment-debtor-petitioner is against the order dated 13.03.93 passed by Senior Assistant Judge, Narail Sadar in Title Execution Case No. 5 of 1989. 2. Opposite party Sree Mati Dasi obtained a decree in Title Appeal No. 349 of 1984 by judgment and decree dated 31.7.89 reversing the judgment and decree dated 29.12.81 passed in Title Suit No. 139 of 1970. After the said decree opposite party filed Title Execution Case No. 5 of 1989 for recovery of possession in the decretal 10 decimals of land in that execution case the process server could not deliver possession in the decretal land as he could not ascertain the same without an Advocate Commissioner. Thereafter decree-holder opposite party No. 1 filed an application for delivery of possession in the decretal land demolishing the structures of the petitioner. Upon that application by the impugned order executing Court directed the decree-holder to deposit Taka 200.00 as Advocate Commissioner's fee and observed that Executing Court has no power to add in the decree the relief of delivery of possession by demolishing structures. 3. It appears from the decree of the Court of appeal below that the decree-holder opposite party obtained a decree declaring her title in the suit land and recovery of khas possession in 10 decimals out of the same by removing the defendant-petitioner therefrom. It further appears from the schedule of the writ of delivery of possession that the said 10 decimals of land has been mentioned as to be situated by the side of 29 decimals of acquired land from the southern side of the CS plot No.8. There should have been no difficulty to find out the side land on the part of the bailiff specially when there was structure of judgment-debtor-petitioner standing thereon. 4. Under section 2(16) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act land includes "houses or buildings and also things attached to the earth". In view of the same there should not be any difficulty to give delivery of possession to the decree-holder-opposite party in the decretal land even if it is found that petitioner has raised some structures on the said land. However, structure standing in the said 10 decimals of decretal land having not been decreed in favour of the decree-holder-opposite party, judgment-debtor petitioner is at liberty to remove the same before the delivery of possession. Otherwise the same will go with decretal land. 5. As to the objection regarding non- specification of the said 10 decimals of land in the appellate decree it is necessary to mention that out of 96 decimals of land of the suit plot No.8 an area of 29 decimals from the southern side was acquired by the Government for road and plaintiffs title in the remaining 67 decimal has been decreed. As the judgment-debtor-petitioner forcibly dispossessed the decree-holder opposite party from 10 decimals of land from the southern side of suit land during pendency of the suit, she filed an application on 13.4.77 for recovery of khas possession in the said land. Court of appeal below after detailed consideration of the same, declared title of the opposite party in the entire 67 decimals of suit land and directed to deliver possession to her in the said 10 decimals of land by removing the petitioner therefrom there is no vagueness in the decree. If it is read with the appellate judgment and decree of the trial Court then it becomes clear to understand. Whenever executing court finds any difficulty to understand the decree it can look to the relevant judgment which gave rise to the decree for clarification and appreciating the decree properly. It is not for fun that a decree is passed by the Court. Court always passes a decree to give relief to the aggrieved party. So on technical and flimsy grounds execution of the decree should not be frustrated. Moreover petitioner's claim of title in the suit land having been negative by the Court of appeal below he cannot object to delivery of possession from 10 decimals of land from which he has been directed to be removed raising flimsy objection of non- specification of the said land in the appellate decree. I, therefore, find no merit in the contentions raised by the learned Advocate for the petitioner and no illegality in the impugned order resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs and order of stay granted earlier stands vacated. End.

lawyer:
Mia Abdul Gafur, Advocate ----- For the Appellant.
Asrarul Hossain with Iftekhar Ahmed, Advocates ----- For the Respondent No.1
parties:
Ayub (Md) ------ Appellant
vs
Sonali Bank and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment: Md. Sirajul Islam J: This appeal by the plaintiff is against the judgment and order dated 3.8.85 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st. Commercial Court, Dhaka rejecting the plaint of the Title Suit No. 32 of 1984 of his court. 2. One Mr. Md. Ayub as Managing Director of Bengal Agricultural Implements and Steel Products Industries (Private) Ltd. being plaintiff filed title Suit No. 201/84 in the court of Sub-Judge, 3nd Court, Dhaka against Sonali Bank and for a declaration that the claims of the defendants are wrong, illegal, unjust and excessive and that the plaintiff is not bound to pay the same and that disposal of the raw materials as described in the schedule to the plaint is illegal. 3. The plaintiffs’ case, in short, is that the Bengal Agricultural Implements and Steel Products Industries (Private) Ltd. is a limited Company incorporated in Bangladesh under the Companies Act, 1913 and that the plaintiff Mr. Md. Ayub is representing the Company as its Managing Director. The plaintiff imported "Hot Rolled Steel Flat Bar" as raw materials for the use in his factory through the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 at a value of Taka 6,44,772.00 by mortgaging the property of the plaintiff and paying the L/C margin at the time of opening the LIC and then on arrival of the said goods it was kept, in the custody of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in the premises of the factory of the plaintiff on an AAM account. The plaintiff also brought experts from the foreign country for survey and proper funning of the factory and industry of the plaintiff with the permission of the Bangladesh Bank at L/C value with charges of Taka 1,64,170.98 as service charge on cash credit of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 against deposit of margin. Then the plaintiff gradually obtained loans from the defendant-Bank by pledging the materials of the plaintiff as mentioned in the plaint on cash credit account and also made gradual payments on different dates. The plaintiff by making gradual payments to the Bank lifted some raw materials. But the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 being dissatisfied with the mode of payment issued legal notice dated 2.1.83 through his Advocate Mr. Mohammad Ali, demanding Taka 38,86,872.39 from the plaintiff within 15 days, failing which the defendant will sell out the plaintiffs goods in auction. 4. That on receipt of this legal notice, the plaintiff informed the defendants that he was going to dispose of his property at Dhanmondi which will take some time and as such, the delay in making the payment of the defendant's dues is beyond the control of the plaintiff. In spite of the request of the plaintiff, the defendant on 14.2.83 invited tenders for selling the pledged goods and raw materials of the plaintiff in auction. That the defendants after putting the plaintiffs goods including raw materials in auction, has informed the plaintiff by their letter dated 26.4.83 that they have got the highest bid at Taka 13,81,902.00 and has offered the plaintiff to take delivery of the goods on payment of the said amount within 7 days, failing which they will deliver the same to the highest bidder and will sue the plaintiff for recovery of their remaining dues of Taka 40,66,690.63 from the plaintiff. That the claims of the defendants are wrong and illegal and that they are not legally entitled to realise the same. That the plaintiff has so far paid Taka 15,75,875.00, but that the defendants without adjusting the same are now claiming a wrong, illegal and an excessive amount. That the plaintiff has been requesting the defendants to allow the plaintiff to make part-payment and that the plaintiff is always willing to pay the actual and lawful dues of the defendants if their claims are rectified. Due to some reasons beyond their control, the plaintiff could not so long clear up the dues and requested the defendants to give the plaintiff some opportunity to clear up their actual dues gradually. But the defendants did not at all consider the same and they are now going to deliver the pledged raw materials to others. That the cause of action of the suit arose first on 2.1.83 when the defendant issued legal notice and then on 26.4.83 and thereafter on 6.5.84 when the defendants refused to accede to the plaintiffs prayer for part payment and lastly, on 3.6.84 when the defendants threatened the plaintiff to put the pledged goods in auction and to deliver the same to the auction bidders. Hence the suit for declaration as mentioned above. 5. The defendant-Bank appeared in the suit and filed a petition under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 12.7.84 praying for rejecting the plaint of the suit on the allegation that the plaintiffs suit is not maintainable as being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act without a prayer for consequential relief. The plaintiff filed a written objection against the prayer of the defendant and then the court fixed a date for hearing the petition in presence of both the parties. In the meantime, the Title Suit No. 201 of 1984 was transferred to the Sub-Judge and 1st Commercial Court; Dhaka for disposal and was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 32 of 1984 vide order dated 22.12.84. Thereafter, in the court of Sub-Judge and 1st Commercial Court, both the parties appeared arid different dates were fixed for hearing the petition under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and ultimately the petition was heard on 3.8.85. The learned Subordinate Judge of the 1st Commercial Court after discussing the facts and circumstances of the case, rejected the plaint of the plaintiffs Title Suit No. 32 of 1984 holding that the suit is hit by the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act vide his judgment and order dated 3.8.85. 6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with this judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge of the 1st Commercial Court, Dhaka dated 3.8.85, the plaintiff has preferred this first Appeal against the respondent-Bank. 7. Mr. Mia Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-appellant, has argued that the learned Subordinate Judge has erred in law in rejecting the plaint under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure holding that the suit is barred by law without prayer for consequential relief. The learned Advocate argued that the suit is not hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as because the plaintiffs suit being a suit for simple declaration, it is not necessary for the plaintiff to pray for any consequential relief and as such, the learned Sub-Judge is not justified in rejecting the plaint on that ground. In support of his argument, the learned Advocate referred to a decision in the case of Fazlul Karim vs. Agrani Bank and others reported in 45 DLR 375 and said that it has been held therein that a suit for simple declaration was maintainable without any further relief. It appears that, that was a case for simple declaration that the dismissal of the plaintiff from his service under the defendant was malafide, illegal, void and inoperative and for a declaration that the plaintiff was still in service under the defendants on the allegations that before passing the order of dismissal, the plaintiff was neither supplied with a copy of enquiry report nor he was asked to show cause against the penalty proposed to be inflicted on him. 8. Mr. Mia Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant, next argued that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in rejecting the plaint of the suit on the ground of non- maintainability for want of consequential relief without giving the plaintiff an opportunity to amend the plaint and to pay the ad valorem Court Fee. In support of this argument, the learned Advocate referred to a decision in the case of Sk. Md. Junaid & others vs. Turner Morrision & Co. Ltd. reported in 26 DLR 111 and said that it has been held therein that the plaint should not be hastily rejected without giving the plaintiff opportunity to amend the plaint. It appears, that was a case for declaration that the defendant-petitioner Nos. 1-4 are agents under opposite parties Nos. 2-5 for and on behalf of the plaintiff and for recovery of money on account of damages and losses sustained by the plaintiffs and for other reliefs. The defendant Nos. 1-4 filed a petition under Order 7 rule 11 CPC for rejection of the plaint, but the learned Sub-Judge rejected that petition by giving a judgment. On revision, their Lordships observed as follows: "Rejection of a plaint is not identical with dismissal of a suit. Rejection under rule 11 does not preclude a fresh suit under rule 13 CPC. But still rejection of a plaint should not be hastily made without affording opportunity to the plaintiff either to cure the defect or to amend the plaint." 9. Mr. Mia Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant relying on a decision in the case of National Bank Ltd. vs. Haroon Malik and others reported in 42 DLR 103 again submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge was not justified in rejecting the plaint of the plaintiffs’ suit. That was a suit for simple declaration that the plaintiff was a sponsor Director of National Bank Ltd, the defendant No. 1 and that the plaintiff is entitled to be a shareholder of the same Company on payment of his required subscription claiming that he was one of the original- sponsors of the Bank. Their Lordships, in that case, observed as follows: "The suit was filed on the basis of a loss of contingent right that the plaintiff an alleged promoter, was left out in the formation of the proposed Bank. Such a promoter has always a cause of action for filing the suit." 10. By a consideration of the facts and circumstances of the instant case before us as stated in the plaint, it will appear that the facts and subject matter of the case are quite different from the facts and subject matter of the cases as referred above. Not only that, the facts of the instant case before us are peculiarly unusual about which we shall discuss later on. 11. Mr. Asrarul Husain, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the defendant Bank respondent, has, on the other hand, argued that such a suit as framed in the plaint under consideration for mere declaration without consequential relief is not maintainable and, as such, the learned Subordinate Judge is quite justified in rejecting the plaint of the suit. The learned Counsel further argued that the plaintiff has prayed for a further declaration that the disposal of the raw materials of the plaintiff is illegal and void and, as such, without making at least prayer for permanent injunction for restraining the defendants from disposing of the raw materials, the suit for simple declaration would be hit by the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as because such a declaration in the absence of any injunction would be infructuous. The learned Counsel, in support of his argument, has referred to a decision in the case of Burmah Eastern Ltd. vs. Burmah Eastern Employees Union and others reported in 18 DLR 709. That suit was a suit for simple declaration. Their Lordships in the Revision case took the view as under: "If as a result of the provisions of law, the suit is barred, it would be barred under law, although, strictly speaking, it may not be specifically barred by law in express terms. The court should, in such case, reject the plaint under its inherent power." 12. It appears that the principle of law laid down in the above quoted case is applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case before us. 13. Now coming back to the facts of the instant case, it will appear by a reading of the plaint that the plaintiff has stated in paragraph 12 of the plaint that the cause of action of his suit arose on different dates and lastly, on 3.6.84 when the defendants threatened the plaintiffs to put his goods in auction and to deliver the goods to the auction bidder. It appears that the plaintiff has given different dates for a cause of action but has not stated in the plaint the facts on which his claim against the defendant-bank is based. For proper appreciation of law, we feel it necessary to quote below the provisions of Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Rule 11. The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases: "(a) where it does not disclose cause of action: (b) where the relief claimed is undervalued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the court, fails to do so: (c) where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so: (d) where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law: 14. It will appear from the provision contained in the above quoted clauses (a) and (d) respectively that the plaint can be rejected where it does not disclose a cause of action, and where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law. The cause of action has been defined in clause (e) of rule 1 of Order 7 as the facts constituting the cause of action and when it arose. It will thus appear that not only a date for a cause of action is to be given in the plaint but also the facts constituting the cause of action for the plaintiff against the defendant are necessarily to be mentioned in the plaint. But by a reading of the plaint of the plaintiff, it will appear that the entire plaint is full of facts which constitute a case of the defendant-Bank against the plaintiff to the effect that the plaintiff took a huge amount of loan from the defendant- Bank, although the exact amount of loan is not mentioned, and that he could not make payment within the due date for reasons beyond his control and that he made a prayer for part payment to the defendant and that the defendant's claim as mentioned in the legal notice served upon plaintiff is excessive. 15. All the above facts as stated in the plaint constituted the defendant-Bank's case against the plaintiff, but not the plaintiffs’ case against the defendant. The plaintiff did not also state in his plaint as to how much excess demand has been made by the defendant against the plaintiff in the legal notice served upon the plaintiff. If the defendant's demand is excessive and illegal then what will be the exact and legal amount which the plaintiff is liable to pay to the defendant, has not been stated anywhere in the plaint. In the absence of any such specific statement of facts on which the plaintiffs claim against the defendant is based, it will mean that the facts as stated by the plaintiff in the plaint did not constitute any specific cause of action of the plaintiff against the defendant. Mere mention of some dates in the plaint as cause of action of the suit is not enough to make out a case of the plaintiff against the defendant. We are therefore, of the opinion that the plaint in question as framed is not a plaint in the eye of law. So, this plaint can be rejected on the ground of non-disclosure of a specific cause of action against the defendant. 16. The plaintiff made a prayer in his plaint for a declaration to the effect that the threatened disposal of raw materials of the plaintiff is illegal, but did not make any prayer for injunction restraining the defendant from disposing of raw materials. In such circumstances, the defendant can safely dispose of the raw materials of the plaintiff without any hindrance and therefore, any such decree for declaration will be infructuous. 17. Moreover, the gist of the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is that any person entitled to any legal character or to any right as to any property, may institute a suit against any person denying his right or title, for such a declaration. But the plaintiff has not stated anywhere in his plaint as to what is his 'legal character' or 'status' conferred by law enabling him to make such a prayer for declaration against the defendant. On the other hand, it will appear that the defendant-Bank has a definite legal claim against the plaintiff. In view of such facts and circumstances of the case, we are inclined to hold that the declaration, as prayed for by the plaintiff in his plaint, is not covered by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. This is no plaint in the eye of law and hence it will be barred under law. Therefore, such plaint can be rejected under the inherent power of the court. 18. By a perusal of the impugned judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge dated 3.8.85, it appears that he has stated in his judgment that a mere decree for declaration in such a case without any consequential relief will be a nullity and, as such, the suit would be hit by the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. On this finding the learned Subordinate Judge has rejected the plaint under Order 7 rule 11 CPC. 19. By a careful consideration of all the facts, circumstances and the principles of law as discussed above, we are of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly rejected the plaint of the suit in question and we find nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment and order dated 3.8.85. 20. In the result, the appeal is dismissed with costs. 21. In view of the above decision, the connected Civil Rule No. 56(F)/1985 being infructuous is disposed of, and the stay order is hereby vacated. Send down the lower court records together with the copy of this judgment to the court below immediately. End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 26.6.89 passed by the High Court Division, Rangpur Bench in Civil Revision Case No. 399 of 1984).
full_judgment: Mustafa Kamal J : This appeal by leave by the appellant Assistant Custodian, Enemy Property, Vested & Non-Resident (L&B) and Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue). Pabna is from the judgment and order dated 26.6.89 passed by a learned Single Bench of the High Court Division. Rangpur Bench in Civil Revision No.399 of 1984discharging the Rule. 2. Md. Abdul Halim Miah obtained an ex parte decree on 12.8.59 in OC Suit No. 15 of 1959 from the 2nd Court of Munsif, Pabna. He instituted OC Execution Case No. 3 of 1962 which was dismissed for default on 2.5.63. Four other Execution Cases, namely, OC Execution Case Nos. 9/62, 3/63, 5/66 and 15/67 were filed by him. but all of them were dismissed for default, the last Execution Case having been filed on 27.12.67 and having been dismissed for default on 6.4.68. Respondent Abdul Mannan, a son of the decree-holder Md. Abdul Halim Miah, as the next friend of his father, filed another OC Execution Case No. 5 of 1977 on 26.8.77 with a petition for condonation of delay under sections 5 and 6 of the Limitation Act on the ground that the decree-holder could not proceed with the earlier Execution Cases owing to his insanity. 3. The present appellant filed an objection under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure whereupon Miscellaneous Case No. 38 of 1978 was started. 4. The appellant's objections were that the decree-holder was not an insane person and that his son Abdul Mannan has no legal right to represent him as his next friend and that the execution case was barred by limitation as it was not filed within 3 "years of dismissal of OC Execution Case No. 15 of1967 on 6.4.68. The appellant's further case was that the judgment-debtors Gour Gopal Saha and others left for India before the 6th September, 1965 and the suit property was treated as vested property.The decree-holder at first prayed for release of the suit property but ultimately gave up his prayer and Look lease of the structures standing on the suit plot in the name of his wife. Ameda Khatun with effect from 3.12.65 When the appellant issued notice upon Ameda Khatun directing her to deposit the arrear lease money the decree-holder, his son and wife collusively filed the present Execution case. 5. The learned Munsif dismissed the appellant's objections under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 31.1.79 on the finding that the decree-holder was insane since 1968 and that there were no defects or laches in the present Execution Case. The appellant preferred an appeal. Miscellaneous Appeal No. 7 of 1979, which was allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge. Pabna by judgment and order dated 17.12.79 and the case was remanded to the Executing Court to determine the date from which the decree-holder went mad on the finding that there was no basis in its finding that the decree-holder was insane since 1968 as no witness was examined to prove this fact. On remand the learned Munsif again dismissed Miscellaneous Case No. 38 of 1978 on 5.12.80. The appellant again took an appeal, Miscellaneous Appeal No. 120 of 1980 and the 1st Court of Additional District Judge, Pabna by judgment and order dated 8.8.81 allowed the appeal and again sent back the Miscellaneous Case on remand to the Executing Court for a decision as to whether the objector-appellant was a representative of the judgment-debtors. The learned Munsif again dismissed the Miscellaneous Case on 8.12.83 holding that the decree-holder was insane at the time of the judgment. On a further appeal by the objector-appellant. Miscellaneous Appeal No. 28 of 1983, the learned Additional District Judge, Pabna dismissed the appeal holding that the decree-holder had gone mad before the expiry of the period of limitation of 12 years from the date of decree dated 12.8.59 and that the period of insanity was rightly condoned by the Executing Court under sections 5 and 6 of the Limitation Act. 6. The High Court Division in revision refused to interfere in the matter after holding that since disability of the decree-holder continued with the fresh execution proceeding started by decree-holder's son Abdul Mannan the finding of the Courts below regarding condonation of delay cannot be questioned" and that "section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure has no manner of application in this case" and that "OC Execution Case No. 5 of 1977 though filed after expiration of 3 years from the date passed in Execution Case No. 15 of 1967, it cannot be said that execution case is hit by limitation". 7. Leave was granted to consider the appellant's submission that the High Court Division erred in law in holding that section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure has no manner of application in this case inasmuch as section 48 CPC prescribed the maximum period within which the last execution case is to be instituted. 8. Mr. Md. Moksudur Rahman, learned Advocate for the appellant submits that there are two provisions governing limitation for applications to execute a decree or order. Article 182 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act provides a period of 3 years, starting from the several dates specified in the 3rd Column and section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure fixed an outer limit of 12 years for execution of the decree or order. An execution application has to satisfy both these requirements, with the result that it would become barred under section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure if presented beyond 12 years, and even With in that period to avoid the bar under Article 182, the decree or order has to be kept alive by successive applications within 3 years. 9. Although the respondent-decree-holder has entered appearance we could not allow his learned Advocate-on-Record to make any submission as no concise statement has been filed by the respondent 10. As already observed the decree-holder obtained the decree in OC Suit No.15 of 1959 on 12.8.59 and the decree-holder's son Abdul Mannan as his next friend filed the latest Execution Case NO.5 of 1977 on 26.8.77 with an application for condonation of delay under sections 5 and 6 of the Limitation Act. Clearly therefore the decree-holder's next friend filed the last Execution Case more than 18 years after the decree was obtained. 11. In support of his submission that the last Execution Case was barred by section 48 CPC Mr. Moksudur Rahman has relied upon some decisions ail of which are not relevant. This Court has, however, already pronounced itself on this point in the case of Bangladesh Jatiya Samabaya Bank Ltd. vs. Sangbad Daily Paper and others, BCR 1983 (AD) 418. The said decision was given on consideration of the cases of Md. Abdur Rahim and others vs. Sree Sree Gredhari Jeo. 27 DLR (Dhaka) 72. Pingle Venkata Rama Reddy vs. Kakaria Buchanna and others. AIR 1963 Andhra Pradesh (FB) 1 and Lalji Raja and Sons vs. Firm Hansraj Nathuram, AIR 1971 (SC) 974. This Court approved of the approach of the then Dhaka High Court in the afore-cited cases in 27 DLR (Dhaka) 72 and affirmed that both section 48 CPC and Article 182(2) of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act provide the period of limitation for the execution of a decree. The Civil Procedure Code fixes the longest period whereas the Limitation Act fixes the earliest period to take the first step in execution and the subsequent steps known as steps-in-aid. This Court also affirmed the further view of the then Dhaka High Court that an application for execution has therefore to satisfy first Article 182 of the Limitation Act being the earliest period prescribed and then also section 48 CPC which prescribed the maximum period of limitation. If the execution petition is hit by any of the two provisions it is to fail. 12. It has been noted in the said decision of ours that to remove an anomaly section 48 CPC has been repealed in India by section 29 of the Limitation Act, 1963 and in place of Article 182 of the First Schedule, the period of limitation for the execution of a decree is now governed by Article 136. 13. We therefore accept the submission of Mr. Moksudur Rahman that the latest Execution Case No. 5 of 1977 filed on 26.8.77 is barred by section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that the High Court Division erred in law in holding that section 48 CPC has no manner of application in this case. The appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. Miscellaneous case No. 38 of 1978 is allowed and the respondent's Execution Case No. 5 of 1977 is dismissed as being barred under section 48 CPC. End.

vs.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 22nd and 29th April, 1993 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1366 of 1992)
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ: The main question raised for decision in this plaintiffs appeal by leave is whether a family court has power under sub-section (5) of section 16 of the Family Courts Ordinance 1985 (Ordinance No. XVIII of 1985, briefly, the Ordinance, to direct payment of any money to be paid under a decree passed by it during execution proceeding. The High Court Division has answered the question in the affirmative and it will be seen at the end that the question, not a very difficult one, has been answered correctly.

2. The appellant as plaintiff instituted family suit No. 35 of 1988 in the Family Court (Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Comilla) claiming dower and maintenance from the defendant-respondent. The suit was decreed on 13-6-89 for an amount of Taka 1,77,575.00 Taka 1,75,000.00 as dower and Taka 2,575.00 for maintenances for the period of iddat. The decree was drawn up on 17-8-89 under section 16(1) of the said Ordinance.

3. The respondent preferred family appeal No. 24 of 1989 before the District Judge, Comilla against the aforesaid judgment and decree but the appeal was dismissed by judgment and decree dated 17-4-1990.

4. On 19-10-89 the appellant filed family decree execution case No.7 of 1989 under section 16 (3) (b) of the Ordinance. The respondent filed an application under section 16(3)(a) praying for monthly instalment of the attachable portion of his salary for satisfaction of the decree. The family Court rejected his application taking the view, inter alia, that it was the option of the decree-holder to follow any procedure permitted by law to obtain satisfaction of the decree. The respondent took an appeal to the District Judge, Comilla against the said order, Family Court appeal No. 27 of 1990, and the learned District Judge, by his order dated 9-8-1990, dismissed the appeal on the ground that it was not maintainable. The respondent then took a revision from the order of the learned District Judge, Civil Revision No. 1676 of 1990, before the High Court Division and obtained a Rule but there was no order of stay of the execution proceeding; even then the execution case was stayed by the executing Court. On the prayer of the appellant, however, the stay of the execution case was vacated whereupon the appellant prayed for an order of stay in the pending revision case. The High Court Division granted a limited stay on condition of payment of Taka 50,000.00 by order dated 27-2-92. The respondent did not comply with the order of the High Court Division and instead filed an application for withdrawal of the revision case which was allowed by the High Court Division and the Rule was discharged on 16-3-92 for non-prosecution. Thereafter on 17-3-92 the respondent filed an application in the execution case, this time under section 16(5) of the Ordinance, praying for monthly instalment alleging that he was a service-holder and except his salary he had no other assets and as such, it would not be possible for him to satisfy the decree except by way of making payment by instalments. On 21-3-92 the decree-holder appellant was absent and the family Court upon considering that the respondent had a net monthly salary of Taka 5,227.00 permitted him to deposit in favour of the decree-holder the first instalment of Taka 3,575.00 and then a monthly instalment of Taka 2,500.00. The appellant filed objection against the said order but the family Court, by its order dated 19-4-92, rejected the same, inter alia, upon view that the decree-holder could lake an appeal against the order allowing instalment. The appellant instead of taking an appeal moved the High Court Division in revision and obtained a Rule in Civil Revision No. 1366 of 1992. A learned Single Judge, by the impugned judgment and order dated 29 April, 1993, upon hearing the parties discharged the Rule holding that in enforcing a decree for money the Court may on the prayer of the judgment-debtor direct payment of the decretal amount in suitable instalments, that such a stage comes after the delivery of judgment as provided in section 15 and that the impugned order of the family. Court dated 21-3-92 and 19-4-92 suffered from no legal infirmity resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

5. This appeal has arisen out of the aforesaid judgment and order and the question raised as indicated above, out of the aforesaid circumstances.

6. Md. Ozair Farooq, learned Advocate-on-Record for the plaintiff-appellant, has made a two-fold submission. His first contention is that a family Court may direct under section 16(5) of the Ordinance any money to be paid under a decree in instalments only at the time of passing of the decree and not thereafter i.e. during the execution of the decree. His second contention is that even if it is permissible for a family Court to allow instalments in course of an execution proceeding, it cannot do so as an executing Court, for the authority to allow instalments has been vested with the family Court as a trial Court.

7. Ozair Farooq in developing his second submission has argued that a Court executing a decree has no power to alter or vary the terms of the decree. An order directing instalments is an order which varies the decree. In support of his contention that an executing Court is not competent to direct payment of decretal amount by instalments he has referred to several decisions; namely, Gobardhan Prashad vs. Bishunath Prasad AIR 1921 Patna 340, Gobardhan vs. Dau Dayal AIR 1932 Allhabad 273 (FB), Bilimoriars, Central Bank of India AIR 1943 Nagpur 340 (FB), J Krishnareddy vs. B Ramagopalaiah AIR 1985 Andhra Pradesh 49.

8. For an answer to the question raised in this appeal it is necessary to examine the provisions of section 15 and 16 of the Ordinance which relate to writing of judgment and enforcement of decree and are as follows:

15-Writing of judgment.-(1) Every judgment or order of a Family Court shall be written by the presiding Judge or from the dictation of such Judge in the language of the Court and shall be dated and signed by the Judge in open Court at the time of pronouncing it.

(2) All judgment and orders which are appealable shall contain the point for determination, the decision thereon and the reason therefor.

16. Enforcing of decrees.-(1) A Family Court shall pass a decree in such form and manner, and shall enter its particulars in such register of decrees as may be prescribed.

(2) If any money is paid, or any property is delivered, in the presence of the Court in satisfaction of the decree, it shall enter the fact of such payment or delivery in the aforesaid register.

(3) Where the decree relates to the payment of money and the decretal amount is not paid within the time specified by the Court, the decree shall, on the prayer of the decree-holder to be made within a period of one year from the expiry of the time so specified, be executed-

(a) as a decree for money of a Civil Court under the Code, or

(b) as an order for payment of fine made by a Magistrate under the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (Act V of 1898)

and on such execution the decretal amount recovered shall be paid to the decree-holder.

(3A) For the purpose of execution of a decree under sub-section (3)(a), the Court shall be deemed to be a Civil Court and shall have all the powers of such Court under the Code.

(3B) For the purpose of execution of a decree under sub-section (3)(b), the Judge of the Family Court shall be deemed to be a Magistrate of the first class and shall have all the powers of such Magistrate under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898), and he may issue a warrant for levying the decretal amount due in the manner provided in that Code for levying fines, and may sentence the judgment debtor, for the whole or any part of the decretal amount remaining unpaid after the execution of the warrant to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three months or until payment if sooner made.

(3C) When a decree does not relate to payment of money, it shall be executed as a decree, other than a decree for money of a Civil Court and for that purpose the Court shall be deemed to be a Civil Court and shall have all the powers of such Court under the Code.

(4) The decree shall be executed by the Family Court passing it or such other Family Court to which the decree may be transferred for execution by the Court passing it and in executing such a decree the Court to which it is transferred shall have all powers of the Family Court passing the decree as if the decree were passed by it.

(5) The Court may, if it so deems fit, direct that any money to be paid under a decree passed by it be paid in such instalments as it deems fit.

9. It may be observed that in section 20 of the Ordinance it has been laid down that save as  otherwise expressly provided by or under the Ordinance the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure except sections 10 and 11 shall not apply to proceedings before the family Courts.

10. Order XX CPC relates to judgment and decree which evidently does not apply to a proceeding before the Family Court. Even then it will be useful to look into the provisions for payment by instalments under a decree as provided in the general law i.e. the Code of Civil Procedure. Order XX rule 11 CPC is as follows:

11. (1) Where and in so far as a decree is for the payment of money, the Court may for any sufficient reason at the time of passing the decree order that payment of the amount decreed shall be postponed or shall be made by instalments, with or without interest, notwithstanding anything contained in the contract under which the oney is payable.

(2) After the passing of any such decree the Court may, on the application of the Judgment-debtor and with the consent of the decree-holder, order that payment of the amount decreed shall be postponed or shall be made by instalments on such terms as to the payment of interest, the attachment of the property of the judgment-debtor, or the taking of security from him, or otherwise, as it thinks fit.

11. It is clear from the above that under sub-rule (1) the authority has been given to the Court to allow payment of the decretal amount by instalments for any sufficient reason at the time of passing the decree. Under sub-rule (2) the authority to allow instalments may be exercised on the application of the judgment-debtor and with the consent of the decree-holder even after the passing of the decree. For an application for instalments under sub-rule (2) the limitation under article 175 of the Limitation Act is six months from the date of the decree.

12. The decisions cited by Mr. Ozair Farooq are in connection with the powers of the Court to allow instalments under rule 11, Order XX CPC. Those authorities support the view, there are contrary decisions also, that an executing Court is not competent to allow instalments and such, power vests only in the Court which has passed the decree. This view has been taken apparently following the well-settled proposition that an executing Court cannot go behind the decree. The said decisions, in the first place, are not apt for the present, for we are considering in this case a special statute laying down special provisions relating to judgment and enforcement of decrees.

13. It has been noticed that under the general law the trial Court may allow payment by instalments even after the passing of the decree under certain conditions. Let us see whether sub-section (5) of section 16 of the Ordinance has authorised the family Court to allow instalments after the passing of the decree. The words "to be paid under a decree passed by it" occurring in the sub-section leave no manner of doubt that the family Court is also authorised to direct payment by instalments as it deems fit even after the passing of the decree. We feel no hesitation therefore to dismiss the first contention of Mr. Ozair Farooq that the family Court can allow instalments only at the time of passing of the decree and not thereafter i.e. during execution proceeding. Mr. Farooq having noticed with us the language of sub-section (5) and the provisions under the general law as referred to above has ultimately veered round the view that it is permissible for the family Court to allow instalments even after the passing of the decree. The difference that we find between the general provisions and those provided in section 16 sub-section (5) is that whereas under the former the power is hedged by certain conditions including one of limitation but under sub-section (5) there is no such condition except that the power should be exercised "as it deems fit" i.e. in exercise of a proper judicial discretion. The power is wider under sub-section (5) and may be used either on application by a party or suo motu so long as the decree remains unsatisfied.

<u>14. As to the second contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant that a family Court can allow instalments only as a trial Court and not as an executing Court, it appears to be an argument in tautology because sub-section (4) of section 16 provides that the decree shall be executed by the Family Court passing it or by such other Family Court to which the decree may be transferred for execution by the Court passing it and in executing such a decree the court to which it is transferred shall have all powers of the Family Court passing the decree as if the decree were passed by it. Since a decree passed under the Ordinance can be executed only in the Family court passing the decree, there is only but one court in which a proceeding under the Ordinance is started and concluded ending in the execution of decree or otherwise as the case may be. When a prayer for instalments is made by the judgment-debtor in course of the execution proceeding he cannot but make it before the family Court which passed the decree (the executing Court being the same). In view of the provisions of sub-section (4) there is no scope for raising the question as to the competence of the Court allowing instalments under sub-section (5). Call it the executing Court or the trial Court, it is nonetheless the Family Court which passed the decree and its power to allow instalments even after passing of the decree is undoubted.</u>

15. We, therefore, entertain no doubt that the question raised in this appeal must be answered in the affirmative and the High Court Division has committed no wrong.

16. Leave was also granted to consider another submission of the appellant that in any view of the matter the family Court ought not to have allowed instalments by its order dated 21-3-92 inasmuch as it had already refused the prayer for instalments earlier by its order dated 9-5-90. The argument is that the Court cannot sit over its own order as if by way of an appeal. Mr. Farooq also argued that the plaintiff would stand to gain if the decretal amount was paid at a time and allowing instalments to the defendant caused prejudice to her

17. It has been noticed that the defendant respondent took an appeal against the first order dated 9-5-90 and the learned District Judge having dismissed the appeal as not maintainable took a revision to the High Court Division but ultimately did not proceed with the same and instead filed another application before the family Court on 17-3-92 for allowing instalments which was granted.

18. Miah Abdul Gafur, learned Advocate-on-Record for the respondent, submits that the defendant's first application which was rejected by order dated 9-5-90 was filed under section 16(3)(a) and the second application dated 17-3-92 was under section 16(5) of the Ordinance. The purpose of the first application was different and it was necessary because the appellant-decree-holder started execution under section 16(3)(b) of the Ordinance which was more onerous for the defendant. Mr. Gafur has explained his point by saying that the appellant had maliciously adopted the course under the Code of Criminal Procedure for realising the decretal dues and so the defendant was obliged to file a petition for following the course under the Code of Civil Procedure as provided in section 16(3)(a). Referring to the order of rejection dated 9-5-90, he submits that it is wrong to say that the defendant made the same prayer for allowing instalments after it was rejected by order dated 9-5-90.

19. It is admitted that the decree-holder started the execution case under section 16(3)(b) i.e. she wanted the execution to proceed under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 and an order of arrest was made by the Magistrate. The defendant in his earlier petition under section 16(3)(a) in effect prayed for an order for execution of the decree to be made under the Code of Civil Procedure which was refused on the ground that it was for the decree-holder to choose the procedure for execution of the decree. It will not be fair to say that the defendant was making the same prayer for instalments which was rejected earlier. Even otherwise it is possible that more than one application may be made for allowing instalments if the facts of any particular case justify making of a second application after the first application has been rejected. It is found that before allowing instalments in the present case the family Court directed the respondent to produce from the authority a certificate of his pay and upon furnishing of such certificate the Court allowed his prayer for instalments in exercise of its discretion. There is no reason to think therefore that the discretion has been wrongly exercised in the circumstances of the case. Having regard to the facts as noticed above it will not be correct to say that the family Court sat over its order or that the discretion has been improperly exercised in allowing instalments to the defendant.

The contentions raised by the appellant fail and accordingly the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 109 of 1998.
lawyer:
Shamsul Hoque Siddique, Advocate-on-Record------For the Petitioners. 
Not represented------The Respondent.
parties:
Zainal Abedin & another  ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Md Abdur Rahim  ------ Respondent.
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 3-8-1997 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Order No. 4455 of 1997).
full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque J: Judgment debtor- petitioners seek leave to appeal from judgment and order dated 3-8-1997 passed by Single Judge of the High Court Division in Civil Order No.4455 of 1997 summarily rejecting the revisional application.

2. Respondent obtained decree on 28-7-1987 in Title Suit No.241 of 1986 against the petitioner for perpetual injunction restraining them from interfering with his peaceful possession of the suit property and/or from forcibly entering into the suit land. Thereafter, petitioners having attempted to forcibly enter into the suit land violating the decree of injunction respondent filed Miscellaneous Case No.8 of 1993 under rule 32(1) of Order 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sylhet. Petitioners contested the said case by filing written objection denying the allegations and asserting that they are in possession of the said land on the basis of gift from one Hazi lrfan Ullah and they have not violated the decree. Trial Court allowed the case on 31-7-1995 holding that judgment debtor-petitioners violated the decree of injunction and directed that they suffer Civil Imprisonment for 3 months and also attached their property for 6 months. Being aggrieved by the same petitioners filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 67 of 1995 and after hearing the said appeal was dismissed by judgment dated 30-3-1997. Being aggrieved by the same petitioners moved the High Court Division in civil revision and by the impugned judgment and order the petition was summarily rejected. Being aggrieved by the same petitioners have filed this petition seeking leave to appeal.

3. Learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that in view of the conflicting decisions by two Single Judges as to the maintainability of a case under Order 21 rule 32(1) of the Code for enforcement of a decree of perpetual injunction as reported in 33 DLR 207 and 12 BLD 323 leave should be granted to resolve the aforesaid conflicts.

4. In the case of Kad Banu and ors vs Hajera Khatun and ors 36 DLR (AD) 183 Executing Court attached the properties of the judgment debtors for alleged disobedience of a decree for perpetual injunction. District Judge in revision set aside the order of the executing court holding that an application under Order 21 rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable. On further revision under the repealed provision of section 115(3) of the Code, High Court Division made the Rule absolute. Leave was granted at the instance of the judgment debtors by this Division to consider the question whether a petition under Order 21 rule 32 of the Code was maintainable. The appeal was allowed and the case was sent back to the trial Court to give an opportunity to the parties to prove that the defendants judgment-debtors had wilfully disobeyed the order of injunction impliedly holding that application under Order 21 rule 32 of the Code was maintainable. A Division Bench of the High Court Division with one of us and presided over by Ismailuddin Sarkar J heard a reference made by DM Ansaruddin Ahmed J to resolve the conflicting decisions of different Single Benches as to the maintainability of an application under Order 21 rule 32 of the Code. The said Division Bench relying on the aforesaid decision of this Division held that such an application is maintainable.

<u>5. So, there is no question of conflicting decisions still creating confusions. Since the pronouncement of the aforesaid decisions an application under Order 21 rule 32 of the Code for violation of a decree for injunction is maintainable and the Single Bench decisions holding that such an application is not maintainable have no force at all.</u>

6. In view of the above decisions we find no merit in the submission.

The leave petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Muzibur Rahman, Advocate ----- For the Appellants. 
PC Guha, Advocate ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Parimal Chandra and others ------ Appellants
vs
Shaheda Begum and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 28-11-91, passed by the District Judge, Barguna in Review Case No. 3 of 1991 under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, arising out of the judgment passed in Title, Appeal No. 31 of 1990 allowing, the Review Case and setting aside the judgment delivered by it on 14-4-91 dismissing the appeal on contest and affirming the decree passed by the learned trial Court.

2. Short facts leading to the case are that, the appellants as plaintiffs instituted a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Barguna being Title Suit No. 18 of 1987, praying for setting aside the ex parte decree dated 6-7-78 passed in Title Suit No. 116 of 1977 It was contended by the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 18 of 1987 that the ex parte decree dated 6-7-78 passed in Title Suit No. 116 of 1977 was obtained by the defendants by fraudulent suppression of all legal processes and by practising fraud upon the Court and, as such, the same is liable to be set aside. It has been contended that for the first time on 19-6-87. they came to learn that defendant Nos. 1-3 of the suit managed to obtain the ex parte decree dated 6-7-78 in Title Suit No. 116 of 1977 fraudulently and collusively and hence the suit for a declaration that the said ex parte decree is collusive, void and of no legal consequence.

3. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations of the plaint and contended, inter alia, that the suit is barred by limitation and it is bad for defect of parties. It has also been contended that the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. It was further contended that the suit is hit by the principle of res judicata. It was contended that the summons of the case was duly served upon the defendants of Title Suit No. 116 of 1977, including the present plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2, but they did not contest the suit as they had no prospect therein. It was further contended that the plaintiffs have no title and possession in the suit property, which is owned and possessed by them on the basis of purchase by registered sale deeds dated 24-3-75 following which they duly got into possession therein. Thereafter, they mutated their names in respect of the suit property and since then they have been paying rent regularly to the Government Acquired Estate.

4. At the trial, the plaintiffs examined three witnesses while the contesting defendants also examined three witnesses and exhibited documents in support of their respective case.

5. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence before him was pleased by the impugned judgment dated 31-3-99 to decree the suit on contest.

6. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree, the contesting defendants took an appeal before the District Judge, Barguna being Title Appeal No. 31 of 1990, and the learned District Judge was pleased by his judgment dated 14-4-91 to dismiss the appeal on contest and affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree, the appellants Mst Shahida Begum and Md Mosarraf Hossain, respondent Nos. 1 and 2 before this Court, filed a review application before the learned District Judge, Barguna being Review Case No.3 of 1991 under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

7. The learned District Judge by his impugned judgment dated 21-1-91 allowed the review case and set aside his judgment and decree dated 14-4-91 passed in Title Appeal No. 2 of 1990 dismissing Title Suit No. 18 of 1987. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid impugned judgment, the, plaintiffs preferred this appeal before this, Court.

8. Mr Md Mozibur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants, submits that the learned District Judge evidently erred in law in travelling beyond the scope of review as envisaged by Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and sat over his, own judgment by way of rehearing of the appeal and the same has occasioned failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned District Judge was manifestly wrong in practically re-hearing the appeal in the garb of review and set aside his own clear findings, arrived at in the appeal after full-dressed hearing of the contending parties on illegal and irrelevant considerations. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Court of appeal below evidently erred in law in passing the impugned judgment basing on materials not brought on record legally and on wholly inadmissible pieces of evidence, clearly falling outside the purview of review under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the same has occasioned failure of Justice.

9. Mr PC Guha, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents, on the other hand, submits that although it was not proper for the learned District Judge to go into the details of the merit of the appeal, yet in substance he was right in allowing the review case on its own merit and, as such, the impugned judgment does not suffer from any illegality occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned District Judge committed no illegality in reviewing his earlier judgment on grounds, which were not taken into consideration at the time of hearing of the appeal, which materially affected the ultimate fate of the appeal and; as such, the impugned judgment and order have not occasioned failure of justice.

Point for determination

10. The only point for determination in the appeal is whether the learned District Judge was justified in allowing the review case?

Findings and decision

11. The learned Advocate appearing for the appellants has placed before me the impugned judgment dated 28-11-91 passed in Review Case No.3 of 1991, the judgment dated 14-4-91 passed in Title Appeal No. 31 of 1990 and the judgment dated 31-3-90 passed by the learned trial Court in Title Suit No. 18 of 1987.

12. It appears that the learned Subordinate Judge on detailed discussion and proper appreciation of the evidence on record decreed on contest Title Suit No. 18 of 1987 by his judgment dated 14-4-90. Being aggrieved, the contesting defendants took an appeal before the District Judge, Barguna being Title Appeal No. 31 of 1990 and the learned District Judge, on hearing the parties at length dismissed the appeal on contest by an elaborate judgment dated 14-4-91. Both the learned trial Court and the learned District Judge, as the appellate Court, on consideration of the evidence on record, concurrently found that the impugned judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 166 of 1977 was obtained on fraudulent suppression of the summons upon the defendants. The learned trial Court clearly found in his judgment dated 14-4-91 that the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 116 of 1977 was obtained by suppression of the summons, both in the normal process as well as by registered post by falsely showing the address of the appellants at different places where they usually reside. The learned District Judge, on appeal, also found that the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 116 of 1977 is a nullity in view of the fact that it was passed against some dead persons. To fortify his conclusion regarding his conclusion that the impugned decree in Title Suit No. 116 of 1977 was obtained fraudulently, the learned District Judge reproduced the finding of the trial Court in respect of the evidence of PW 1, which reads a follows:

“হাতেম আলী এবং আবুল হোসেসের পিতার নাম গঞ্জে আলী কিনা স্মরণ নাই। জ্ঞানপাড়া সাকিনের গঞ্জে আলী নামে কোন লোককে চিনি না।”

13. On further scrutiny of the evidence, the learned District Judge clearly found that the defendants of the present case do not even know defendant Nos. 11-13 of Title Suit No. 116 of 1977, who were dead at the time of trial of the said suit. The learned District Judge further found that the appellants could not say if defendant Abul Hashem of Title Suit No 116 of 1977 is alive or dead. After detailed consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, the learned District Judge clearly found that the ex parte decree in Title Suit No. 116 of 1977 was obtained by fraudulent suppression of the summons upon the defendants and, as such the said decree is liable to be set aside.

14. While reviewing his own judgment the learned District Judge re-opened the entire case and resorted to re-hearing the appeal in the garb of review. In doing so, he not only set aside his own findings arrived at on detailed discussion of the evidence but also set at naught his ultimate decision basing on matters which were not legally brought on record, being quite oblivious of the scope of a review.

15. The supreme consideration for the Court in deciding the fate of the present case was to decide whether the ex parte decree in Title Suit No. 11 of 1977 was obtained collusively and fraudulently by suppression of the legal processes and not to judge the propriety of the said judgment on any other count. It was obviously no business of the learned District Judge to discover legal infirmity in the said judgment on the alleged ground of absence of possession of the plaintiffs of that suit in the suit land and that too on speculative considerations based on totally inadmissible evidence. It is unfortunate that while deciding a review case the learned District Judge found illegally in the judgment of Title Suit No. 116 of 1977 on the basis of an enquiry report submitted by a Magistrate in connection with a criminal case. This betrays on the part of the learned District Judge a sense of colossal indifference and total lack of the application of a judicial mind into the facts and circumstances of the case and the law regulating review. It is to be noted in this connection that the learned trial Court on due consideration of the evidence of PWs 1-4 for the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 18 of 1987 clearly found the plaintiffs possession in the suit land. So, the finding of the learned District Judge in the review case that the plaintiffs of that suit being out of possession in the suit land, the decree obtained therein is a nullity is wholly unwarranted and is the product of mere surmises and conjectures. Evidently, the learned District Judge erred in law in making the said finding as a ground for review. The finding of the learned District Judge 9tIrt the point of limitation in Title Suit No. 18 of 1987 in reviewing his judgment is also found to be based on extraneous and illegal considerations and, as such, not sustainable in law.

16. The power of review as visualized by section 114 is to be traced to Order 47(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, which contains the prescribed conditions and limitations in terms of the requirements of that section, A review is not available simply in the interest of justice", unless the case falls within the purview of the powers contained in the relevant provisions of law. It must be clearly understood that a review is not a re-hearing of a case for re-opening a closed chapter. It is only available in certain well-defined circumstances, namely, where some important evidence has been discovered, which could not, in spite of due diligence, have been known to the party or being produced at the time of hearing or the Court has overlooked some material questions of fact or law which would have a good bearing on the decision of the case or there is otherwise some apparent mistake or error on the face of the record, The ground that the Court has fallen into an error in deciding a particular question or that an important ground which could have been urged but was nor urged at the original hearing, is no ground for review. the power of review is essentially an enabling provision available to a party to ask for reviewing a judgment or order under specific conditions circumscribed by Order 47,rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, it must be exercised within the strict limits set by law and not lavishly at the pleasure of the Court. The finality that attaches to a judgment or order passed by a competent Court on hearing the contending parties cannot be lightly interfered with in review in the garb of re-hearing the case. The consistent judicial view of the superior Courts of the sub-continent is that a review is never meant or, allowed to be utilized as an opportunity for re-opening or re-hearing the matter which is already closed by final judgment:

<u>17. The learned Advocate for the appellants has referred to me the case of Abu Bashar vs Mehar Khatun, reported in 35 DLR 6, the case of Khairuzzaman and others vs. Noor Hossain, reported in 9 BLD; 453, the case of Nurul Hossain vs Government of Bangladesh, reported in 47 DLR (AD), 108 in support of his submissions. The ratio decidendi of all these decisions does not support his contention. "Mistake or error apparent on the face of the record" has been consistently held as an error which stares in the face so that it requires no elaborate argument and scrutiny. No such, case has been made out in the instant case to give a helping hand to the learned District Judge in reviewing his own judgment passed on merit.</u>

18. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record, I am constrained to hold that the learned District Judge failed to address himself to the moot question involved in a review application and instead allowed himself to be swayed by illegal and irrelevant considerations, travelling beyond the scope of Order 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure and illegally resorted to hearing the appeal afresh. For the reasons stated above, I find sufficient substance in the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the appellants and these are accordingly sustained. The appeal succeeds.

19. In the result, the appeal is allowed without any order as to cost and the impugned judgment and order dated 28-11-91 passed by the learned District Judge, Barguna in Review Case No. 3 of 1991 setting aside his, own judgment and judgment and decree dated 14-4-91 passed in Title Appeal No. 31 of 1990 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 31-3-90 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Barguna in Title Suit No. 18 of 1987 are hereby set aside. Title Suit No. 18 of 1987 of the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Barguna stands decreed. The judgment and decree dated 14-4-91 passed by the learned District Judge, Barguna in Title Appeal No. 31 of 1990 affirming the judgment and decree dated 31-3-1990 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Barguna in Title Suit No. 18 of 1987 decreeing the suit are maintained.

Send down the lower Court records immediately.

End.

lawyer:
Md. Hannan, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md. Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ---- For the Appellants. 
Shamsul Haque Siddique, Advocate-on-Record ---- For Respondent Nos.1-8.
Not represented ----Respondent No.9.
parties:
Surat Sarder and others ----- Appellants
vs. 
Afzal Hossain and others ----- Respondent
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 11-5-93 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision Case No. 348 of 1990).
full_judgment:
Md. Abdur Rouf J: This appeal by leave by the plaintiffs is from the judgment and order dated May, 11, 1993 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.384 of 1990 discharging the Rule and upholding thereby the judgment and decree passed on October 11, 1989 by the learned Subordinate Judge, Meherpur allowing Title Appeal No.156 of 1986 and setting aside the judgment and decree dated August 3, 1986 passed by the learned Munsif, Gangni decreeing. Title Suit No.117 of 1985.

2. The plaintiff-appellants instituted the aforesaid suit for declaration of their title to and confirmation of possession in the suit land on the averments, inter alia, that they became owners of the suit land by inheritance as well as by purchase from the transferees of the original owners, Hemanta Kumar, Ranginimoyee Dashya and Soudamoni Deshya, recorded in CS Khatian No.390, Mouza Kazipur, PS Gangni, Meherpur; that during SA Operation the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of the Government and they instituted TS No.50 of 1969 for correction of record and got a decree; that in pursuance of the said decree the SA records were corrected in their names and they have been possessing the same on payment of rent; that having come to know on 28-4-85 the conspiracy of the defendants to dispossess them from the suit land they instituted a proceeding under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and ultimately the Upazila Magistrate dismissed that case on 10-6-85 with the observation that the dispute should be resolved between the parties in the civil Court; that thereafter the defendants again conspired to cut and take away forcibly the paddy and jute grown by the plaintiffs in the suit land and they having come to know on 15-6-86 of such conspiracy of the defendants brought the aforesaid suit with a prayer for injunction.

3. Defendant-respondent No.I-8 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the case of the plaintiffs. Their case, inter alia, is that one Nilkanta and Rajmoni auction purchased the suit land in execution of a rent decree passed in Rent Suit No.163/39 and they exchanged the same with one Fakir Mohammed's properties, situated in India, through a Power of Attorney executed on 29-3-63 in favour of said Fakir Mohammed and they being the successors of said Fakir Mohammed are the owners in possession of the suit land.

4. Considering the evidence of 7 PWs and 3 DWs and the documentary evidence, the trial Court decreed the suit in part declaring plaintiffs' title to 3.20 acres of land out of 3.53 acres. On an appeal, preferred by the defendants, the lower appellate Court reversed the decree of the trial Court and dismissed the suit holding, inter alia, that the plaintiffs had failed to show the cause of action for the suit in the plaint. The plaintiffs then moved the High Court Division in revision and obtained Rule in the aforesaid civil revision case. A Single Bench of the High Court Division concurred with the lower appellate Court's views and discharged the Rule by the impugned judgment and order.

5. Leave was granted to consider the submissions made for the appellants, that the lower appellate Court upon misconception of law and facts as to the cause of action for the suit and its maintainability in its present form wrongly dismissed the suit and the learned Judge of the High Court Division also suffered from the same misconception resulting in a failure of justice.

6. Mr. Md. Hannan, learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-appellants submitted that in the plaint, the plaintiffs clearly stated in paragraphs 2 and 5 that the defendants conspired to dispossess them from the suit land by cutting and taking away forcibly the paddy and jute grown by them, which the plaintiffs came to know on 15-6-85 and, as such, the cause of action for the suit arose from that date. The trial Court framed issue No.1 as to the maintainability of the suit and held that the suit as framed was maintainable and accordingly, decreed the suit in part declaring the plaintiffs' title in respect of 3.20 acres of land out of 3.53 acres. Mr. Hannan further submitted that the lower appellate Court although found that the plaintiffs on the basis of Ext.6, the decree of Title Suit No.50/69, Kabalas Ext.2 and 4 dated 25-4-56, Kabala Ext.3 dated 1-7-68 and Kabala Ext.5 dated 27.2.84 proved their title to 2.99 acres of land but wrongly held that they are not entitled to the decree as prayed for and that they ought to have filed a suit for permanent injunction. The learned Advocate submits that the learned Judge of the High Court Division upheld the decree of the lower appellate Court upon an identical misconception of law that the cause of action for the suit having been shown to be a mere threat to dispossess the suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession was not maintainable.

7. Mr. Shamsul Haque Siddique, learned Advocate-on-Record appearing for respondent Nos.1-8, submitted that in view of the provisions of Order VII, rule 1(e) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the lower appellate Court on consideration of the evidence on record dismissed the suit holding that the suit was bad for want of cause of action, as the plaintiffs did not make any allegation in the plaint that the defendants disputed their title to the suit land. The learned Judge of the High Court Division has lawfully upheld that judgment and decree of the appellate Court.

<u>8. The term "cause of action" has not been defined in the Code of Civil Procedure. Rule 1(e) of Order VII of the Code only provides that besides other particulars, mentioned in different clauses of Rule 1, the plaint shall contain the "facts constituting the cause of action and when it arose". The cause of action for the suit ordinarily thus, means the cause which leads the plaintiffs to bring a legal action. The incidence of cause of action must be antecedent to the bringing of the suit at a time when the right to sue arose for the first time. It consists of the entire set of facts which gives rise to a legal action and is to be proved to entitle the plaintiff to succeed in the suit. It has little relation either to the defence to be taken by the defendant or the nature of relief to be prayed for by the plaintiff in the suit.</u>

<u>9. In the case of Chand Kour & another vs. Partab Singh & others, 16 ILR (PC) 98(102), arising out of a suit for declaration that a certain gift made in 1879 was inoperative, their Lordships of the Privy Council observed (judgment delivered by Lord Watson), "the cause of action has no relation whatever to the defence which may be set up by the defendant, nor does it depend upon the character of the relief prayed for by the plaintiff. It refers entirely to the grounds set forth in the plaint as the cause of action, or, in other words, to the media upon which the plaintiff asks the court to arrive at a conclusion in his favour".</u>

<u>10. In the case of Tar Muhammad & Co. vs. Federation of Pakistan and others, 9 DLR 197, a Division Bench of the then Dacca High Court, comprising of Amin Ahmed, CJ and Chakraborty, J. (judgment by Amin Ahmed, CJ) the plaintiff, a businessman of Karachi brought a suit for damage at Chittagong Court against Karachi Steam Navigation Co. Ltd. defendant No.2, their local agent defendant No.3 and the Federation of Pakistan as defendant No.1 for short delivery of rape-seeds at Chittagong Port which they had imported from Karachi. On the objection raised by defendant No.2 as to the jurisdiction of Chittagong Court on the ground of rubber-stamp clause on the bill of lading that the disputes were to the settled in the Courts of Karachi the trial Court after deciding the preliminary objection returned the plaint under Order VII, rule 10 CPC. In dismissing the appeal preferred by the plaintiff their Lordships made the following observation:</u>

<u>"Now the cause of action, as it means, denotes a bundle of essential facts which is necessary for the plaintiff to prove before he can succeed in his suit. It has no relation whatever to the defence which may be set up by the defendant, nor does it depend upon the character of the relief prayed for by the plaintiff. It refers entirely in the grounds set forth in the plaint as the cause of action, or, in other words, to the media upon which the plaintiff asks the Court to arrive at a conclusion in his favour."</u>

<u>11. In the present case it is already mentioned that the plaintiffs in paras 2 and 5 of the plaint clearly stated that to prevent the breach of peace in respect of the suit land they had to bring a criminal proceeding against the defendants under section 144 CrPC in April 1985 and the same was ultimately dismissed on 10-6-85 by the Upazila Magistrate. Thereafter the defendants again conspired to dispossess them from the suit property which they came to know on 15-6-85 and that was the date for cause of action for the suit. The contesting defendants denied the plaintiffs right, title, interest and possession in the suit land and claimed their right, title, interest and possession therein. Plaintiff No.1 as PW 1 also asserted those facts in his deposition. The lower appellate Court palpably misconceived the meaning and purport of cause of action for the suit, although the plaintiffs had clearly stated in the plaint a bundle of facts which constituted the cause of action for the suit and plaintiff No.1 as PW 1 also asserted those facts in the deposition. The trial Court in consideration of such evidence of record also found possession of the plaintiff in the suit land But the lower appellate Court did not reverse this finding. The learned Judge of the High Court Division, thus, clearly fell into an error upon an identical misconception of law as to the meaning and purport of cause of action for the suit in holding:</u>

"I am in agreement with the lower appellate Court that the cause of action was the threat held out by the defendant-opposite parties to dispossess the plaintiffs from the suit land by reaping the paddy, the jute grown on the suit land. As the threat shows that the plaintiffs were in possession of the suit land and the lower appellate Court also found the title to and possession of the suit land with the plaintiff the present suit for declaration of title to and confirmation of possession is not maintainable".

Both the judgments and decrees of the lower appellate Court and the High Court Division are not sustainable in law. We find substance in this appeal. Accordingly it is allowed without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division and the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court are set aside and the judgment and decree dated 3-8-86 passed by the learned Munsif in Title Suit No.117 of 1985 decreeing the suit are restored.

End.

lawyer:
AY Salehuzzaman, Advocate ----- For the Plaintiff- Petitioners.
